#6165. The 8 Best Solar Generators Provide Reliable Backup Power in a Pinch

These tested and researched models from Jackery, EcoFlow, Anker, and other trusted brands are the ones we stand behind and recommend.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Power stations (i.e., solar generators) have become increasingly popular because they are easy to run, cost less over time than gas generators, and offer eco-friendly, emission-free operation, especially when paired with a solar panel. Some are small and compact, ideal for off-grid adventures, while larger ones are able to back up critical home circuits during a blackout.

Unlike fuel-based generators, solar generators can’t create electricity in real time. They’re giant battery packs, not true generators, and need to be recharged using alternating current (AC) power or solar panels, the latter of which often takes many hours in ideally sunny conditions.

Despite those distinctions compared to portable generators, there’s nothing more convenient than a power station for charging or running everything you need for day-to-day life—phones and laptops, lights, and even a small appliance or two. Plus, it’s nice to have a device that doesn’t produce carbon emissions and replenishes itself freely from the sun’s rays. Whether you’re seeking a highly portable option or need one that’s heavy-duty enough for extended use, these are the best solar generators we’ve tested and researched to date.

To pick the best solar generators, we tested some of these power stations for charging capacity, ease of use, weight, and different use cases. Our picks were reviewed by Popular Mechanics editor Brad Ford, who provided input for the larger-capacity units. Other models on this list were reviewed by test editor David Dritsas or freelance writer Maggie Slepian.

Our primary concerns were portability and convenience. Ease of use was also important—was the display easy to read? Did the screen readouts make sense? Bonus points if we could tell how much power is available at a glance. In the past few years, these criteria have become easier to meet. There are now plenty of compact, affordable units that have better charging capabilities than before.

Very few power stations of this size can handle as much solar input power as the Bluetti Apex 200. With two input types—low-voltage XT60 (up to 1,000 watts) and high-voltage MC4 (up to 2,000 watts)—it can accept up to 3,000 watts of solar power. If you had the panels and ideal weather, you could fully charge this station in less than 2 hours—even faster than plugging it into the wall. That’s impressive.

It also balances nicely between being a portable station and a home backup solution. It offers 3,200 watts of continuous power (it says 3,600 on the front, but that’s only if it’s connected to an expansion battery). We were able to power a refrigerator for a full 27 hours on a single charge, and estimated the battery efficiency at 90 percent, which is very good. Meanwhile, the 2,560-watt-hour battery capacity is expandable by adding up to six additional batteries. Using Bluetti’s largest battery, the B500K, you could build a massive 33-kilowatt-hour system.

While 3,600 watts isn’t enough to power a whole home, you could power a couple of circuits through a manual transfer switch using the 120-volt 30-amp output. But keep in mind that there’s no 240-volt support, so you can’t use it to power high-voltage appliances like electric dryers.

As a portable station, the Apex 200 has a lot to offer. At 59 pounds, it’s not too hard to move around the house or in and out of a vehicle. And there are several great DC power options, including a bank of USB outlets (two are high-power USB-C) and both 10- and 30-amp, 12-volt outputs. We also love that the AC ports can individually be turned on and off using the mobile app; this helps improve overall runtime.

Since very few stations can match its max solar input capacity, we concluded that the Apex 200 is definitely a top choice for anyone who wants a power station that can recharge using the sun’s rays, but also offers the versatility of being used on the road or at home.

Full Bluetti Apex 200 Power Station Review

This model replaces the original Jackery 1000, but many of the same observations made of the first model still apply. The new version has a slightly higher capacity of 1,070 watt-hours and uses a newer lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery, which is a newer battery technology that offers a longer lifespan (4,000 cycles versus 500 cycles for this model) and better performance in extreme temperatures.

Expert Maggie Slepian used the previous model on a media trip where she had to keep multiple camera batteries charged during a weeklong outing. She found that while the capacity was lower than you'll find with others on this list, it actually powers items for longer than some higher-capacity models. She also charged her photographer’s camera batteries while charging the power bank on solar power (it was a very sunny winter day), which proved effective and efficient.

The newer V2 model has seven ports, including three AC outlets, two USB-C ports (one 30-watt and one 100-watt), a 12-volt car port, and one standard 18-watt USB-A outlet. It charges a typical laptop eight times or powers a small refrigerator or an electric cooler for over 15 hours.

The Jackery Explorer 1000 V2 charges with a 200-watt solar panel or a 12-volt outlet in your vehicle while you’re on the move. It has fairly standard charging times, with 11.5 hours in a car outlet, 6.5 hours for solar panels, and just 5.5 hours to fully charge in a wall outlet. This won’t be your best bet for powering larger appliances, but it’s an ideal power station for smaller items and off-grid camping.

This power station takes solar recharging seriously. The Elite 300 can accept up to 1,200 watts of input, which is a high amount for a station this size. We paired it with a 250-watt portable panel and, on a fully sunny day, got around 260 watts of input. That’s the typical efficiency of a portable panel (again, you’ll never get 100 percent). But pair it with some larger panels, and you’ll get even more.

It also boasts an impressive battery capacity of just over 3,000 watt-hours and 2,400 watts of output, which is high for a station of this size. Plus, it includes a 120-volt 30-amp port, which is handy for connecting it to a small RV or pop-up camper, allowing you to run small appliances and water pumps. It’s not enough power to run a heating or cooling system for a significant amount of time, but for lights, small appliances, and other items that need power, this station will deliver.

If there’s one downside we found, it’s that there’s no way to add an expansion battery to increase your capacity. That’s not a huge detractor, but it’s something we’ve seen in stations even smaller than this one. But at the end of the day, the Bluetti Elite 300 solar generator offers the right balance between a midsize power station that delivers a lot of power and run time, and a station that is compact and portable enough to be perfectly suited for an outdoor adventure.

Full Bluetti Elite 300 Solar Generator Review

The EcoFlow Delta Pro is a large portable power station with an output that rivals some gas portable generators. When sold in a bundle with solar panels, like the package with two 220-watt portable panels we tested, it becomes a powerful solar generator. With an output of 3,600 watts, the Delta Pro can charge multiple appliances, and the output has the ability to bump up to 4,500 watts with its built-in X-Boost technology if more power is needed.

To get an idea of the run time, we used the Delta Pro to power a full-size, 25-cubic-foot refrigerator—which it did for a remarkable 51 hours and 24 minutes. When recharged from a standard outlet, it took only two hours and 36 minutes. But it also charges with the included adapter, at electric vehicle charging stations, with a DC car adapter, or with the solar panels that come with the unit. Through the 30-amp connection, you can also connect this to a transfer switch to directly power select circuits in your home.

Like any power station with a large battery capacity, it will take a long time, perhaps nearly two days, to recharge this station using the bundled 220-watt solar panels. The good news is the Delta Pro accepts up to 1,600 watts of solar input, so it can charge faster by connecting more panels.

The heavy-duty wheels and telescoping handle on Anker’s Solix F3000 are easy to use, allow you to stand upright when pulling, and are a dream for people who regularly find themselves moving their power station around, whether it’s at a campsite or to different parts of the house during a power outage.

Along with convenience, this generator is a powerhouse with the capacity to easily run your refrigerator or a greenhouse heater, or keep your RV bright and warm.

We were impressed with Anker’s app, which allows us to check the charging status or power being generated without continually going outside to check. The app also lets you turn the power to the AC and USB ports on and off remotely, keeping tabs on how much energy is being utilized.

The Solix F3000 has 11 ports, including two car ports, an RV-specific outlet, four AC ports, three USB-C charging ports, and two USB-A. In sunny conditions and moderate temperatures, it recharges with a 400-watt solar panel in just a few hours and supports up to 2,400 watts of solar input.

One of Jackery’s most recent solar generators is also its most rugged, able to withstand the elements better than most. It achieves this with an IP65 weatherproof rating, molded rubber port covers, a shockproof enclosure, and a bottom drainage system, which is part of a titanium alloy cooling structure that helps keep water out of the enclosure.

We got a chance to see these features up close and were impressed by them all, as well as a very sturdy enclosure that, thanks to the cooling system design, eliminates any side vents that could allow water to get inside. It feels strong; you could bang this station around without worrying too much about damaging it. The only downside is that this denser construction adds a bit of weight.

As a power station, it delivers 1,800 watts of output with a battery capacity of 1,536 watt-hours. That’s enough power for a weekend camping trip or for running low-powered small appliances and some lighting during an emergency. As a solar generator, it can handle up to 800 watts of input from a portable panel. We paired it with a Jackery 200-watt panel, and it worked well. Overall, if your off-road adventures often get a little dirty, but you need some extra power, the Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station is a good one to have at your side.

Full Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra Power Station Review

The latest version of the Goal Zero Yeti 1500 is a well-designed power station that’s ideal for off-grid camping situations where dust, wind, and potentially wet conditions are always on the table. This 2,000-watt power station is weatherproof with an IPX4 rating and features outlet shields that cover the ports and inputs. Each section is well-lit by an LED light that’s individually turned on or off using a manual button or the mobile app (and will shut off if not used after a certain period).

There’s a healthy number of outputs on the Yeti 1500, including four 120-volt AC outlets, four (two are high-powered) USB-A ports, and four 12-volt connections. We simulated an emergency blackout and managed to run a cable modem with a WiFi router, a lamp, a TV, and a tower fan, while charging a phone and a laptop through the USB-C ports. Given the station’s output and capacity, there was enough power for over two days of use (conveniently shown on the main display), and there was plenty of room to spare for a few more devices.

To test its solar capabilities, we paired the Yeti 1500 with a Nomad 200-watt portable solar panel and connected it using the high-voltage DC input, which accepts up to 600 watts; however, it also features a low-voltage input that accepts up to 300 watts for smaller panel arrays. Because both inputs can be used simultaneously, you could theoretically pair with two arrays for up to 900 watts, which is a high amount of input for a station of this size.

Of course, no portable panel operates at 100 percent efficiency. Even on a sunny, cloudless day with no shade-causing obstructions, the input readings showed anywhere from 125 to 145 watts. After initiating a recharge with only 5 percent capacity left, it would take at least 10.5 hours in those conditions to recharge. That’s actually not bad. An average of about 70 percent efficiency for a portable panel is good.

The Anker Solix C2000 power station can deliver the full 2,400 watts of output to the bank of five AC outlets—something similar stations don’t offer. This allows you to power several things at once, like a refrigerator, toaster, router, and chargers, all at the same time.

During our tests, we were able to take full advantage of this, powering a refrigerator (by itself for up to 18 hours), along with some high-powered appliances, like a four-slot toaster and an electric kettle (though not the last two at the same time).

Another interesting ability of the C2000 is that you can fast charge it from AC power up to 1,800 watts, but that recharging rate remains consistent if you’re powering other devices at the same time (we confirmed this with a wattmeter). For example, we ran a 1,400-watt space heater while still recharging at the full 1,800-watt rate. Other power stations offer similar fast charging but will throttle the amount of power coming into the station while powering devices.

For solar recharging, we were a bit disappointed that this station can only accept 800 watts of input; other stations of this size accept more. But when solar was plugged in, it worked well. We connected it to a 200-watt Anker portable panel, and in full sun, we were getting around 125 to 145 watts of input, which is pretty good as these types of panels go. The C2000 is not IPX-rated for any type of weather resistance, however, so we would not recommend leaving this station sitting outside if the weather turns wet.

Full Anker Solix C2000 Power Station Review

Power stations use watts and watt-hours to express size and capacity. Watts (size) refer to how much power it produces. For example, if you need to run a 900-watt microwave, you’ll need a station that outputs at least that much power (ideally more, since factory specs are never exact).

Meanwhile, watt-hours (capacity) give you an idea of how long devices can be powered continuously, though how much time depends on the amount of power being drawn—watt-hours don’t dictate a set time frame. Higher-powered devices will drain the battery a lot faster than lower-powered ones.

That may seem confusing, but a simple equation gives you an approximate idea of how it works: total watt-hours (of the generator) ÷ watts (of the device) = hours the power station runs.

For example, if you had a power station with a 2,048-watt-hour capacity and wanted to run a 750-watt space heater consistently at its highest setting, it would probably run for around 2.5 hours, so long as nothing else is plugged in. But for a refrigerator, whose power draw fluctuates between 10 and 300 watts (depending on how often the compressor turns on), you might be able to run it for nearly 24 hours.

Keep in mind that manufacturer specs are taken from perfect conditions; in the real world, you’ll likely see slightly less capacity from your power station. If you’re not sure how much power the different devices in your home draw, sometimes it’s written on a label, or you can use a device like a wattmeter.

Just as a power station has specifications on output size and capacity, solar panels are rated by how many watts they produce for a device after they convert the sun’s rays into electrical current (e.g., 100 watts, 200 watts, etc.). Because real-world conditions are never perfect, it’s not uncommon for panels to only output 50 to 75 percent (or even lower) of their total potential.

Your panels must also be within the acceptable input range of the power station. For example, connecting a 400-watt solar-panel array to a power station that only accepts 110 watts of solar input can cause an overload and damage the station.

While weight and size don’t directly correlate to the technicalities of power banks, they impact the convenience of each model. Many camping and overlanding setups have limited space, so the more compact models likely have a higher appeal as a result.

That said, most units weigh at least 10 pounds, and the weight and size increase quickly with greater capacities. Before purchasing, consider where you plan to store the power bank and the space in your vehicle or camper where it will live while you’re on the road. If you plan to use this power bank solely as a home backup option, portability will matter less, but consider how much effort it will take to move it around within your home or in your outdoor space.

I am a low-maintenance camper, and most of my background is in lightweight backcountry travel. That means I prioritize space-saving and ease-of-use, so my go-to power banks have between 250 and 600 watt-hours, and weigh less than 15 pounds.

This is perfect for a weekend trip, with the on-the-go (car or solar) charging capabilities to put my mind at ease for longer trips. Mostly, I’m charging small items, so one charge lasts a long time. However, plenty of people in the van-life and remote-work world are powering their RVs and vans, and relying on multiple laptop charges. For that, I’d recommend one of the larger units.

A solar-powered generator charges and runs almost anything that requires power—it just depends on the capacity. These generators can charge power tools in the shop, laptops for remote work, and personal devices like Bluetooth headphones and speakers.

A solar-powered generator with a higher power capacity can even power household appliances in the event of a power outage. And the fact that these are solar-compatible means you aren’t reliant on the electrical grid to recharge them.

Every unit on our list has multiple charging options, including wall (AC outlet), car (12-volt), and solar. Each input method charges your unit at a different speed, and solar also depends on the conditions. AC power is the fastest, followed by 12-volt, and then by solar (though a larger solar array could potentially be faster than 12-volt).

I try to charge up my power banks whenever I can, so I’m never caught off guard trying to leave on a trip with a dying power bank. If this happens (which it has), I’ll charge it in my vehicle’s 12-volt port while I’m driving, though this is often slower than solar or a wall unit.

Solar power is the most sustainable and typically fastest way to power these—just be sure you have enough wattage in the solar panels to make it effective. I recommend keeping the generator stored with at least an 80 percent charge, and unplugging it once it’s fully charged—keeping it plugged in longer than necessary degrades the battery.

Most units will have a simple readout display showing the remaining battery charge, and it’s a good practice not to allow your battery pack to get below 20 percent.

#6164. Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A comet or a newborn star might explain an odd signal in telescope data. Astrophysicist Isabel Angelo is looking for signals that defy those familiar explanations.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”

Archaeologists discovered a stash of Celtic coins ahead of a construction project for an electrical substation in Hungary.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists in Hungary have discovered a stash of more than 200 Celtic silver coins that are over 2,000 years old. It's one of the largest hoards found there in decades.

Researchers unearthed the coins during excavations ahead of construction for an electrical substation in western Hungary between 2023 and 2025, according to a translated statement from the power company E.ON. The hoard dates to sometime between the late second century B.C. and the early first century B.C.

The coin cache weighs roughly 4.4 pounds (2 kilograms). In today's market, it's worth more than $2,000 as raw silver alone, but its rarity and historical value effectively make it priceless, the statement said.

The site was once part of a farm, and plowing there had unearthed several individual coins in recent decades, the statement said.

During the latest excavations, archaeologists initially found a few coins and then searched the area with metal detectors, which led them to the coin hoard. The treasure had been packed inside a small ceramic vessel and sat about 16 inches (40 centimeters) below ground.

"This is a rarity in Europe," Eszter Kreiter, an archaeologist at Hungary's National Archaeological Institute, said at a news conference, according to local news outlets. She added that the last similar find was made in Hungary in the late 1960s.

The hoard's silver coins are modeled on Greek tetradrachms — a very early type of large silver coin that was introduced in the late sixth century B.C.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The newfound Celtic tetradrachm copies are a type known as "Velem," which are named after Velem-Szent Vid, a fortified Celtic hilltop settlement, or oppidum. Similar coins have been found at that site, which is located about 10 miles (15 kilometers) to the west.

Each coin has a stylized head on one side that probably depicts the Greek god Apollo, and portrays a helmeted rider and horse on the other side.

Artifacts from more than 7,000 years of occupation have been found at the site, including a glass bead (bottom, center) thought to be about 2,500 years old.

The excavations have revealed evidence of more than 7,000 years of occupation at the site, officials wrote in the statement. The artifacts include a nearly 7,000-year-old polished stone chisel used for woodworking and a glass bead with a peacock's eye pattern that seems to have been part of jewelry from the sixth or seventh century B.C.

A Roman-era villa was built at the same site in later centuries, without disturbing the hoard of buried silver, Kreiter said at the news conference.

The site in Hungary's western Szombathely region was excavated between 2023 and 2025 ahead of the construction of an electricity substation.

The villa has long since been demolished, but the excavations enabled the archaeological team to reconstruct its floor plan, including its underfloor heating system, she said. They also found a Roman-era brick with a dog's paw print.

The artifacts from the site will become part of a museum exhibition.

According to Museum Wales, the Celts were loosely related Iron Age peoples descended from Proto-Indo-European speakers. Emerging in Central Europe, Celtic groups occupied much of Central and Western Europe from about the 10th to the first century B.C. The Celtic Gauls were finally defeated by the Romans, led by Julius Caesar at Alesia, now in eastern France, in 52 B.C. The Britons were also Celtic, though most people of Celtic descent would not have recognized that name.

Several modern ethnic groups, including the native Irish and the Bretons of coastal France, trace their descent to the Celts. Regions with strong Celtic origins are sometimes called the "Celtic fringe" of Western Europe.

Writing in the Journal of Roman Studies, the British coin expert Christopher Howgego, an honorary curator and professor emeritus of Greek and Roman numismatics at the University of Oxford, stated that Celtic tribes in the Carpathian Basin, now in Hungary and Romania, started minting their own silver coins after Celtic mercenaries had seen them when serving with Hellenistic armies in Greece and Macedonia.

Howgego has written that the Greek-inspired Celtic coins included adaptations of classical Greek portraits, as well as distinctive Celtic designs. These copycat tetradrachms held very high value for their makers, so they were rarely used for everyday purchases. Instead, they were often hoarded as wealth or buried as ritual offerings.

Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

#6161. Rift grows among Senate Democrats over who will lead in majority

Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin hold a news conference calling for a “bold direction” for Senate Democrats on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

More Democrats emerged Tuesday wanting someone besides Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., to lead their conference in the majority.

But Schumer maintained confidence he would be reelected to the post despite Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., publicly calling for a different leader or a “concrete plan” that provides change.

“I’m confident I will be elected majority leader, and our caucus is really united in focusing on bringing down costs, on ending the corruption, on ending the chaos, on ending the war,” Schumer told reporters Tuesday. “We have great unity in our caucus, and I’ll be proud to lead it.”

Sanders said during a news conference Tuesday the election was about “change and the need for the Democratic Party to move in a new and bold direction.”

“I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader,” Sanders said, calling for an “economy that works for all, not just the people on top.”

“Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction?” he asked. “No.”

Some incoming members and now incumbents have pointed to Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen as one possibility to challenge Schumer. Van Hollen had previously thrown cold water on the idea by saying he was instead “kicking the tires” on a presidential run in 2028 but has recently changed his tune.

A person familiar with Van Hollen’s thinking said he “has received an outpouring of calls on running for majority leader and is now in active listening mode.”

Slotkin did not endorse anyone for leader but said she had a “really productive conversation” with Van Hollen yesterday.

“Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that’s definitely different. I’m a ‘no’ until and unless I see that from anyone,” she said, urging her peers to “withhold quorum” when Senate Democrats hold their leadership elections “until you get that plan and you feel like you have a voice in that plan.”

She urged not just a roadmap for the first 100 days, but ideas for how to “communicate differently.” As for her own future, she said, “I am not actively seeking this job. I’m seeking change.”

Asked about his plans Monday evening, Van Hollen said, “It’s not about me, but I am listening to the thousands of people who have been calling for change, but especially listening to our members, with a particular ear to new members who have just come off the campaign trail.”

“What I’ve said from the very beginning is, we shouldn’t have a coronation. We should have a caucus discussion about what we're going to do with the power and responsibilities that have been invested in us,” Van Hollen said. “I’m in listening mode and haven’t shut the door.”

Van Hollen took it a step further at an event Tuesday in Washington, D.C., criticizing the minority leader and Democrats’ campaign arm over their preferences in some primaries. “Schumer and the DSCC sided with the crypto industry and AIPAC against these candidates,” he said, according to a livestream of the event.

Schumer tried to tamp down the suggestion of a rivalry. “We talk frequently, and we’re united — united in lowering costs, and united in ending this damn war,” he said of Van Hollen.

Others threw their support behind Schumer ahead of the Democratic leadership elections, which are expected to take place in December.

Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., praised Schumer for raising money and recruiting candidates like Sens.-elect Sherrod Brown of Ohio and Roy Cooper of North Carolina to help land at minimum seven seats, and potentially nine if Alaska and Mississippi ultimately swing their way.

“That takes vision. It takes clarity of thought. It takes strategic leadership, and that is what Sen. Schumer has done. And that is why you will see, despite all grumblings, enormous gratitude,” she said.

Gillibrand pointed to candidates like Scott Colom, the Democrat in Mississippi who is currently leading GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a nail-biter of a race. “That wave doesn’t get created by magic. It gets created by hard work and putting the pieces together over years,” she said.

Colom, however, has been noncommittal, telling MS NOW, “Too many of our leaders are from the same areas of the country,” pointing to the Brooklyn roots of both Schumer and current House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to run for speaker on the House side.

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., said he and Schumer have had their differences. But he implied he backs him for majority leader: “At the end of the day, these are historic numbers. It’s time for us to unify. We are going to work together as a caucus to plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think we have the person who I think is going to lead us there.”

Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., said Democrats have “an opportunity to do things differently, and I think we will, regardless of who the leader is. It doesn’t really matter whose name is on the door.”

“Yes,” he said of his support for Schumer, noting that so far, nobody has officially stepped up to the plate. “This is a guy that worked incredibly hard over the last couple of years. I know people have other opinions about this. But we have a mandate to do things and get things done for the American people.”

Mark Schoeff Jr., Paul M. Krawzak and Kelly Livingston contributed to this report.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. #6158. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

R. J. Stern et al. ROVing in the deep: tectonic and magmatic complexities of the Challenger Deep forearc segment, Southern Mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science. 2026. doi: 10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6157. Republicans tap Moreno and Jack to lead Senate and House campaign arms

Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno will chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee during the 2028 cycle. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo)

House and Senate Republicans picked their new campaign chiefs Tuesday, tasking Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack with leading the GOP campaign arms for the 2028 election cycle.

In their new positions, both will spearhead Republicans’ push to win back majorities on Capitol Hill after Democrats seized control of both chambers of Congress by flipping more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats in last week’s midterm elections.

Republicans returned to Capitol Hill this week still reeling from their losses but resisted calls to delay Tuesday’s leadership elections. In the Senate, South Dakota’s John Thune was reelected Republican leader without any opposition, while Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan defeated Louisiana Rep. Steve Scalise in a closed-door, secret-ballot election to lead House Republicans next year.

Moreno will succeed South Carolina Sen. Tim Scott as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee.

“Republicans must enter this next election clear-eyed: the road ahead back to a Republican Senate majority will by no means be easy but the fight has never been so important,” the Ohio senator said in a statement.

Speaking to reporters on Capitol Hill, Moreno described his new role as “a hell of a job.” He said Republicans would be “absolute savages” on ending government corruption and continuing “to work for the American people.”

“I suspect the best tailwind we’ll have is that the Democrats will learn all the wrong lessons,” he told reporters.

Moreno, a close ally of President Donald Trump, is currently serving his first term. He first ran for Senate during the 2022 cycle but dropped out of a crowded GOP primary eventually won by JD Vance. Two years later, buoyed by an endorsement from Trump, he won a contested primary for the state’s other Senate seat and went on to oust Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown that fall.

Brown is poised to return to the Senate after defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted last week in a special election for the remaining Senate term of Vice President Vance. While Ohio has swung heavily toward Republicans over the past decade, Democrats scored big wins in the Buckeye State last week, winning several statewide offices and flipping three seats in the U.S. House.

But assuming he runs again for a full term, Brown will be on the ballot in 2028, setting up what’s likely to be a tense home-state fight.

In an apparent reference to the returning Brown, Moreno offered some Washington advice Tuesday: “Make sure you rent. Do not buy.”

The 2028 Senate map gives Republican pickup opportunities in a handful of swing states, including Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, New Hampshire and Pennsylvania. The party will also be defending battleground seats in Alaska, Iowa, North Carolina and Wisconsin. Also on the Senate ballot are races for Republican-held seats in Kansas and South Carolina, where Democrats scored surprise wins last week.

On the House side, Jack defeated Indiana Rep. Rudy Yakym III to become the next chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee. He takes office after one of the worst elections for the GOP in recent decades and will succeed outgoing NRCC Chair Richard Hudson, who lost his own North Carolina seat last week.

House Republicans face the tough task of cutting into Democrats’ 40-plus-seat majority next cycle. But the party will have a slew of pickup opportunities, given the sheer number of seats Democrats won in historically red territory this year.

Like Moreno, Jack was first elected to Congress 2024, leveraging a close relationship with Trump to win an open seat outside Atlanta. He previously was White House director of political affairs during Trump’s first term and was a senior adviser to the president’s 2024 campaign. Over the past two years, he served as the NRCC’s recruitment chair.

Savannah Behrmann contributed to this report.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

Stephanie Pappas is a contributing writer for Live Science, covering topics ranging from geoscience to archaeology to the human brain and behavior. She was previously a senior writer for Live Science but is now a freelancer based in Denver, Colorado, and regularly contributes to Scientific American and The Monitor, the monthly magazine of the American Psychological Association. Stephanie received a bachelor's degree in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a graduate certificate in science communication from the University of California, Santa Cruz.

This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6153. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

#6152. Independents decide the election, again!

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also shows that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

For example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

Despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

Overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

In the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

According to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top issue concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

Trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic issues and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

Neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

At a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent said the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

#6149. The 7 Best Garage Heaters for Your Workshop

These editor-approved electric and gas models turn chilly spaces warm fast—so you can pull off your gloves and get your projects done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Garages and unfinished basements are often poorly insulated, making them prone to extreme cold in fall and winter. A garage heater can turn this typically frigid space into a warm, practical area for woodworking projects, vehicle maintenance, and more. If you plan to spend time in your garage this winter tackling projects at your workbench, raising the ambient air temperature is a must.

Garage heaters come in various styles, though the most popular models are electric and propane. Electric heaters are convenient and easy to install if a power outlet is nearby. Propane heaters are more portable and can cover more surface area. Natural gas garage heaters are also powerful options for larger garages and can offer long-term heating solutions.

Heaters can benefit not only comfort but also safety. Cold temps can cause condensation to collect on tools and stored items, which may lead to rust and other damage. Wintry environments can also cause car engines and batteries to wear out faster. A well-heated garage protects your investments and provides a warmer, safer place to work.

If you're ready to prep for winter weather, read on for our in-depth reviews of the best garage heaters, followed by the most important things to know before buying.

Although we haven’t tested the models below ourselves, we applied our experience testing space heaters and patio heaters to supplement our search for the best garage heaters. We spent a lot of time vetting features and specs, checking manufacturer websites, gauging prices, and consulting user reviews before deciding which ones made the cut. We spoke with mechanical and electrical engineering experts to understand what makes a great garage heater, and we considered heat types (electric, propane, or kerosene), as well as whether the heaters are permanent or portable.

This 240-volt compact garage heater is the best all-around choice for most spaces, with 7,500 watts of heating power and the option to mount it on the wall or ceiling.

According to the manufacturer, it warms a typical garage or unheated building to between 50 and 85 degrees Fahrenheit and should be installed with a foot of clearance from combustible surfaces.

The garage heater’s adjustable louvers let you direct air where you need it most, and a remote-controlled thermostat is built into the front of the heater. A wall-mounted thermostat is available for the unit as well, but it’s sold separately.

Thanks to its Wi-Fi capability, you can operate this heater from virtually anywhere to ensure your garage is warm when you get home, or to heat the space before you spend time at your workbench. You can turn the unit on and off and set recurring schedules through the app.

The garage heater is rated to warm a 1,000-square-foot area, with an adjustable output of up to 20,000 BTUs. It can be mounted to the wall or ceiling, and its large digital temperature display is easy to read, even from across the room.

But for the price, it’s disappointing that the garage heater doesn’t include wiring.

For a powerful 5,600-watt portable garage heater, we recommend this NewAir model. It’s designed to warm spaces up to 600 square feet, and it includes a 6-foot cord that neatly coils on top of the unit, with brackets to hold it down.

The fan has two settings: automatic (which turns on when the heating element activates) and continuous. You can switch between the two manually.

Use continuous mode to keep air moving in spaces with high ceilings or when you’re operating an air-cleaning appliance, like a bench-top air filter, as it helps push dusty air through to speed up the process.

Designed for outdoor areas like patios, this Briza heater still works well in a garage thanks to its dust-resistant properties. It comes with an adjustable tripod that you can set between 44 and 84 inches tall. Selecting between its three heat settings—900, 1,200, or 1,500 watts—is easy with the unit’s remote control.

The heater has a built-in safety sensor that automatically shuts the appliance off if it tips over. A timer provides additional safety (and energy savings) by automatically shutting the heater off after 1 to 9 hours of operation.

For a compact, affordable garage heater ideal for targeted heating, this propane-fueled unit from Mr. Heater is a great choice. It delivers 4,000 to 9,000 BTUs from a single 1-pound liquid propane canister and can heat up to 250 square feet. It works great on the floor by your workbench or desk.

The heater can run for up to three hours on high, or you can upgrade to a 20-pound tank with a separately sold adapter. The heater’s size and weight make it easy to reposition, and it’s easy to bring with you to a shed, campsite, or other workspace.

This heavy-duty, 240-volt garage heater is ideal for climates with major temperature swings, featuring a two-stage high-and-low heating system.

Its lower heat output suits mildly cool days, while the higher stage can warm garages in single-digit temperatures. It also has a fan mode ideal for increasing airflow in a potentially stuffy garage, plus an energy-saving setting that defaults to the lowest wattage to maintain the desired temperature.

A universal bracket is included for easy mounting to a ceiling or wall, and this heater has a remote-controlled thermostat. The only drawback is that it doesn’t offer much coverage for the price.

If you have an uninsulated wood garage or another minimally insulated space, this large, ceiling-mounted garage heater is worth a look.

It runs on natural gas (a propane conversion kit is included) and, with a built-in electric fan, can warm areas up to 2,000 square feet thanks to its impressive 80,000-BTU output. It also has a powered exhaust that allows for vertical or horizontal venting.

Note that the Big Maxx does not come ready to install; you’ll have to purchase a thermostat, gas hose, fittings, and regulator separately. For most people, it’s best to have a licensed heating-cooling contractor install this garage heater.

There’s a lot to consider when using a heater to keep your garage safe and comfortable. So we picked the brain of Pat Porzio, a mechanical engineer and multi-licensed tradesman (electrical, plumbing, HVAC). He’s also the HVAC manager for Russo Brothers in East Hanover, New Jersey. We also spoke with David Shapiro, an electrician, author, and expert on old house wiring who contributes to electrical product and installation standards.

Both agree on one thing: Your overarching concern in heating a garage is safety. The first words out of both their mouths were identical: “Pull a permit.” That is, if you plan to use a permanently installed electric or gas-fired garage heater, you need to file a building permit for the work—whether you do the work yourself or hire a contractor. Permitted installations are inspected by the town or other authority with jurisdiction over this work where you live, which increases the likelihood of a safe installation.

Aside from pulling a building permit for the electrical work, Shapiro steers homeowners away from any heater without a UL (or other safety-related U.S. testing agency) listing.

Using a 120-volt space heater is simpler; same goes for small propane-fired and kerosene heaters. You don’t need a building permit to use one of these in a garage. Still, there are safe and unsafe ways to use these heaters. For more on that topic, check out our garage heater safety tips below.

As we mentioned earlier, there are a couple of different types of garage heaters. Electric heaters are easier to install, don't require a vent, and are generally safer. But depending on your local electricity rates, they can be more expensive to run. Gas heaters use natural gas or propane, and they can be a more cost-effective option for heating larger garages. They require ventilation, which can be a pain if you don't already have the right setup.

Infrared heaters heat objects rather than the air, so they can be a good companion for localized projects at your workbench. Forced-air heaters use a fan to distribute heat quickly and work well for large spaces, but they require good insulation to run efficiently and may kick up dust around your workshop.

For most garages, an electric heater is often the most viable option because it's easy to install, safe, and effective. But if you have a larger or poorly insulated garage, a gas heater might be the way to go.

“A bigger heater is not necessarily better,” Porzio says. “An oversized heater will short cycle. That is, it will turn on and off too frequently. It satisfies heating demand very quickly and abruptly turns off. A heater that is too small will do just the opposite. It will run and run and never fulfill the heating demand, eventually wearing itself out.”

Before contractors install a boiler or furnace, they perform a series of calculations, called a Manual J, to determine the correct size. While homeowners can get a rough estimate by multiplying the area's square footage by 50 to get the required BTUs, Porzio recommends using simplified Manual J forms online or a sizing tool like those on King-Electric.com and Newair.com.

For reference, a two-car garage will need a heater ranging from 30,000-50,000 BTUs to reach a consistent, comfortable temperature.

Whether you attempt the electrical work or hire it out, Shapiro has two more recommendations. First, don’t install the heater so that a power cord leading to a machine or tool could be draped directly in front of it. The heat can damage the cord.

Second, consider installing a CO alarm in the garage. A CO alarm can make the garage a safer place to work, especially if you’re heating it with gas, and it can also protect the occupants of the house.

Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins, some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought, governed and died thousands of years ago.

Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide invaluable clues about long-lost languages and civilizations. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script, one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

Each type of discovery offers a new window to the ancient world. But which of these archaeological treasures would you most want to uncover? Vote in the poll below and let us know your thoughts in the comments.

#6147. White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter says.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself said that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the new Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability issues, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin said.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.
