#6107. The 7 Best Portable Jump Starters to Bring Your Vehicle Back to Life

The days of needing jumper cables and another motorist to revive your vehicle are over.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you’ve got a dead car battery, you’ll want the option to revive it without waiting for help. According to AAA’s most recent report, of the 27 million calls received across the country for roadside assistance, 7 million of those vehicles had battery trouble. The causes may include anything from neglecting to turn off your car’s ignition or headlights, residing in an extremely cold climate, or even a slowly deteriorating alternator.

A portable jump starter, which is a compact and powerful battery consisting of lightweight lithium-ion, is a handy device that’s faster, safer, and more convenient than jumper cables because you don’t need to find another car with a willing driver.

Like all batteries, lithium-ion cells have different power ratings and can become depleted from repeated use or by sitting idle over time. That’s why before purchasing a portable jump starter, consider these two specs: peak amperage (amps) which conveys how much power a device can deliver, and capacity (rated in milliampere-hours, mAh), indicating how long a device can hold a charge when stored and still have enough power to provide a jump. It’s also important to monitor the charge level on your portable jump starter from time to time. I do this regularly while waiting to fill my gas tank.

There are other convenience features these devices offer, like USB ports to recharge portable electronics and lights for illumination when it’s dark. Many portable jump starters have what’s called a boost button, which I recommend having, as it supplies extra momentary power for severely drained batteries. After several rounds of testing, research, and evaluation, these are the top portable jump starters to buy now.

I’ve owned close to a dozen vehicles during my 30-year-plus career writing about cars and have had plenty of dead batteries. I keep jumper cables in each of my three current vehicles, and now I also have a portable jump starter on board along with a portable tire inflator, dash cam, and Cobra RAD 700i radar detector, which I move between vehicles depending on which I decide to drive.

In short, each device in this roundup can quickly start a vehicle with a depleted battery. While testing each product, I also evaluated its peak instantaneous power measured in amps, power capacity measured in milliampere-hours, the quantity and variety of output ports to charge portable electronics, and extras such as lights and a boost button.

My recommendations are based on a product’s price, capability, and capacity to fit a wide array of vehicles and budgets. I took into account my own experiences with portable jump starters, each brand’s reputation, and for further background, I spoke with fellow car enthusiasts and auto journalists to get their impressions.

With 6,000-amp peak current to jump-start a vehicle with up to a 12.0-liter diesel engine coupled with 27,000 mAh of power capacity, the Gooloo GT6000 is the most powerful device in our guide. The GT6000 offers up to 24 months of standby time—and with that, you get incredible peace of mind. This device can sit unused for long stretches and still be counted on to crank your car when needed. If its battery is depleted, the GT6000 is ready to jump-start a vehicle after just 7 minutes of recharging and is fully recharged in 1.4 hours via its 100-watt USB-C in/out port.

This device also stands out for its generous quantity and variety of charging ports. In addition to a 100-watt USB-C in/out port, it also has a 12-volt/cigarette-lighter cord to recharge its battery in a pinch. A 15 volt/10-amp DC port can be used to power assorted car accessories like portable air pumps and power inverters. There are two USB-A power ports, one rated at 5-volts/2.4-amps and another rated for 5/9/12-volts

The GT6000 is one of only two devices here with an LCD screen, which makes checking battery level, charging output, temperature, and jump-start status quick and easy. There are 10 safety features, in addition to a built-in LED flashlight with three lighting modes (flashlight, strobe, and SOS) that provides illumination when using the device in low-light situations—important so other motorists can see you if you’re stuck on the side of the road.

While the GT6000 admittedly provides more power than most motorists will likely need, and it’s one of the heaviest of our picks, it is without question the best overall jump starter for maximum instantaneous power, long standby time, quick recharging, and plenty of output ports.

The AstroAI S8 isn’t the most powerful jump-starter recommended but it’s one of the lowest-priced and is user friendly and small enough to fit in your car’s glove box or map pocket. Although it taps out on vehicles with anything larger than a 6.0-liter gas or 3.0-liter diesel engine, it’s fine for most vehicles. I’ve kept this in one of my vehicles for months and used it several times to provide jump-starts to others without an issue.

Protection against reverse polarity, overcurrent, overvoltage, overload, overcharge, over discharge, and short circuiting are built in. The AstroAI S8 has two 5-volt/2.4-amp USB-A output ports to charge portable devices and an LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes. It is supplied with a USB A to USB C charging cable to recharge the device.

The interface is one of the most barebones of all the units tested—just a power button and four blue LEDs to indicate power level. It does have a boost button but is the only unit of our selections without a shut-off switch; instead it automatically powers off after 30 seconds.Full AstroAI S8 Portable Jump Starter Review

This is the smallest device I tested (only slightly larger than most smartphones) and the lightest at 1.2 pounds. With 2,000 amps of peak power, the Gooloo GP2000 can jump-start vehicles with up to 8.0-liter gas or 6.0-liter diesel engines and its 12,000 mAh of capacity is impressive for its size and price.

It has 10 safety protection features including short circuit and reverse polarity, and a 400-lumen LED flashlight with normal, strobe, and SOS modes to provide light in dark environments and during emergency roadside stops. It comes with two USB-A outputs—one 5/9/12-volt and one 5-volt/2.4-amp—for charging portable devices, a USB-C charging cable, and a storage case instead of a bag like many portable jump starters at this price.

Like the AstroAI S8, it has only an on-off button. It’s easy to use and has a boost button. I recommend this option for anyone looking for a small, inexpensive, and hassle-free portable jump starter.

With an IP65 water-resistance rating and rubberized casing, the Noco Boost Plus is the portable jump starter I turn to during the rainy season in Oregon—which means anytime other than summer. I go for this one because it has spark-proof and reverse polarity protection for safe use in wet or dry conditions.

Its 1,000-amp peak power rating can start vehicles with up to 6.0-liter gas and 3.0-liter diesel engines. However, its 2,150 mAh capacity is the lowest of any product here, so it may not hold a charge as long as jump starters with a higher capacity. While this is adequate, I don’t recommend a mAh rating any lower.

The Noco GB40’s 100-lumen flashlight is dimmer than that of some of the other units in this roundup but it has the most modes, six total, which include 100-, 50-, and 10 percent; blink, SOS, and strobe. It also comes with a 1-foot USB-C charging cable, but it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A output port for charging your portable electronics.

If you own a large vehicle, the Noco Boost X GBX155 cranks out 4,250 amps to boost batteries instantaneously for vehicles with up to 10.0-liter gas and 8.0-liter diesel engines, and has an impressive 26,750 mAh capacity, just shy of the Gooloo GT6000’s 27,000-mAh spec. A 60-watt USB-C input/output allows recharging from 0-to-100 percent capacity in 2.7 hours to ensure it’s ready to jump-start a vehicle after charging only 5 minutes (slightly faster than the Gooloo GT6000’s 7 minutes.)

I found the Noco Boost X GBX155 more complicated to operate than the other portable jump starters I tested. For example, it doesn’t have a boost button like other units but rather a manual override feature that’s used to jump start severely depleted batteries if the device detects the battery is below 3 volts. Aactivating the feature requires holding the Manual Override button for 3 seconds, which can send the GBX155’s maximum output of 4,250 amps to jump start a vehicle. This Manual Override shuts off the Noco’s automatic spark-proof and reverse-polarity protection so users need to be extra careful to attach the jumper cables correctly (red to positive, black to negative) to avoid damaging the car’s electrical system, and not touch the clamps together, which can create dangerous sparking.

The Noco is heavy, too, at 5.8 pounds. In addition to its 60-watt USB-C input/output, it has only one 5-volt/2.1-amp USB-A port whereas other lower-priced devices have at least two. But you won’t be working in the dark if you are trying to start your battery at night. This device has a 500-lumen LED flashlight that’s the brightest of the portable jump starters in our roundup. Another perk: it’s got an IP65 waterproof rating (with its input/output ports covered) that only the Gooloo GT6000 and Noco GB40 also have.

For motorheads with multiple vehicles and a garage or shop to keep them, the Clore Automotive Jump-N-Carry JNC660 is a worthy device to have on hand. Its 120-volt male receptacle connects to an extension cord so that it can be powered by a regular wall outlet and is always charged and ready.

This device uses a lead-acid battery instead of a lithium-ion one. This makes the battery replaceable, so this device is not ultimately disposable like portable jump starters with a lithium-ion battery. At 18 pounds, it’s by far the heaviest here, but also has the longest (46 inches) and thickest (2-gauge) jumper cables.

With 1,700 peak amps, it’s not the most powerful portable jump starter included but makes up for that with a 22,000 mAh rating which means its internal battery holds a charge longer. A built-in digital voltmeter shows the battery’s state of charge before and after a jump start and it has a DC outlet to power 12-volt accessories such as a tire inflator or power inverter. A notable drawback: It doesn’t have USB output ports.

For years, I relied on a Battery Tender trickle charger to supply a slow, steady current to keep the battery in my classic Chevy Impala SS charged. If you also have a vehicle that sits idle for months on end, check out the Battery Tender Charge N Start 4120. It does double duty as a trickle charger and a jump starter. However, combining two devices in one comes with compromises such as not having output ports to charge portable devices, or a boost button.

With 1,200 amps of instantaneous current, this device can jump start cars with up to 6.0-liter gas or 4.0-liter diesel engines and proficiently cranked the engine on several large and small vehicles during my testing. Its basic push-button interface makes the Charge N Start a breeze to operate. Safety features include spark-proof connection, reverse-polarity protection, and more.

This portable jump starter sends a small amount of current to traditional lead-acid as well as lithium batteries at 4 amps, and an onboard microprocessor maintains the optimal voltage to keep a battery at 100-percent capacity without overcharging during long-term storage. It also includes temperature compensation to handle a range of climates.

Something you may need to think about is its size. Its larger than other trickle chargers I’ve used, which affects placement. Ideally, a trickle charger should be located close to the battery under a car’s hood. The Charge N Start may be too large to tuck away under the closed hood of certain vehicles, but a supplied 6-foot extension cable that attaches to low-profile battery-charging clamps allows locating the device away from the engine on, say, a shelf next to a wall outlet.

The Noco AX65 is another portable jump starter we’ve tested and recommend, but we moved it out of our guide because it’s not singularly a portable jump starter like the others. This is a combo device with a portable air compressor so you can start dead batteries and inflate flat tires. What I like is that the unit doesn’t skimp on either function. The jump starter has an impressive 16,000 mAh capacity and delivers 2,000 amps of peak power while the tire inflator pumps out 67 liters per minute of airflow, which converts to 2.3 cubic feet per minute (cfm)—well above average for the portable tire inflators I’ve tested.

The portable jump starter can crank a dead battery on vehicles with gas engines as large as 8.0 liters and diesel engines up to 6.0 liters. It can be used for SUVs, boats, and snowmobiles. The not-so-good news: It’s short on output ports compared to the other portable jump starters here, and heavy at more than 9 pounds.

Portable jump starters are essentially heavy-duty batteries that come with jumper cables, controls, and accessories like lights, charging ports, and air pumps. Here’s what to look for when shopping for a portable jump starter that fits your vehicle, needs, and budget.

The two most important specs to look for when comparing portable jump starters are peak amperes (amps) and milliampere-hours (mAh). Peak amps indicate the maximum short-term current a device can deliver, while mAh measures how much electrical charge a battery can store.

Bigger is better for both specs, although mAh isn’t always as prominent or even stated with portable jump starters compared to peak amps. About 400 to 600 peak amps is sufficient to jump-start vehicles like cars and crossovers, although large SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles may require up to 1,500 or 2,000 amps. Some portable jump starters come with a boost button that provides roughly 10 additional amps and is helpful when reviving a very dead battery that needs an extra jolt of juice. At least 10,000 mAh of capacity means the battery in a portable jump starter will hold enough charge for 3 to 6 months to deliver 5 to 10 jump-starts.

Portable jump starters are a much safer alternative to using jumper cables to revive a dead battery because connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that can sometimes ignite gas produced by the battery and cause an explosion. Also, if you connect the cables incorrectly, called reverse polarity, it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, portable jump starters have built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity in addition to other safety features and are much less risky and easier to use.

Most portable jump starters also come in handy for recharging phones, tablets, and other portable devices. USB output ports are the most common, but a few devices also provide a 12-volt outlet. While USB ports typically charge at 2.5 to 5 volts, a 12-volt outlet can not only charge a device faster but can also be used to power devices such as portable air pumps and coolers.

If you need to jump-start a vehicle at night, you’ll be thankful your portable jump starter has an LED flashlight. Typically a portable jump starter’s lighting feature also provides strobe or SOS patterns to warn other motorists on the road of your presence.

Look for a portable jump starter with a boost button to give an extra jolt of juice to a very depleted battery when the device’s standard output can’t crank the engine. This surge of power gives you about 15 to 30 seconds to start the car once the boost button is pressed.

A portable jump starter rated for 400 to 600 amps is sufficient to jump-start most passenger vehicles such as cars, crossovers, and smaller SUVs. But for larger SUVs, trucks, RVs, and commercial vehicles you want to look for a device with at least 1,500 to 2,000 amps. Weather also affects a car battery and engine, so if you live in a very cold climate more power may be needed to jump-start a low or dead battery.

Yes and no since it depends on the wide range of passenger vehicles available. A portable jump starter with a lower amp rating can jump-start smaller vehicles such as most cars, crossovers, and small SUVs. But a large SUV or truck with a large engine will require a portable jump starter with a higher amp rating.

Peak power rating (measured in amps) to ensure a portable jump starter has enough juice to crank your vehicle and capacity (measured in milliamp hours) that indicates how long it can potentially hold a charge are the most two important. Other features to look for include the number and types of output charging ports, whether it has a 12-volt output and charging input, a boost button, and a flashlight.

Definitely. Make sure to first read the owner’s manual to understand how your portable jump starter works before connecting it to a car’s battery. When using it, take off any jewelry and wear safety glasses and gloves anytime you work on a vehicle and especially around a battery. Most portable jump starters come with built-in safety features that will issue a warning if they are connected incorrectly. But it’s up to you to double-check that the jump starter’s red/positive and black/negative clamps are connected to the (typically) red positive and black negative terminals of the car battery.

Yes, a portable jump starter is a much safer alternative to using traditional jumper cables to start a vehicle with a dead battery. Connecting jumper cables to a battery’s terminals can cause sparks that have the potential to ignite gas produced by a battery which in some instances can lead to an explosion. And if you connect the cables incorrectly (in reverse polarity) it can severely damage a car’s electrical system. Unlike jumper cables, most portable jump starters come with built-in protection against issues like sparking and reverse polarity and are much less risky and easier to use. Plus, with a portable jump starter you don’t have to find another car—and a driver—like you do with jump cables. That said, I carry a set of jumper cables as a backup.

Researchers knew that cholesterol and blood pressure are important for estimating stroke risk, but a new study suggests these should be measured far earlier in life.

Cardiovascular disease has long been linked to risk factors like high blood pressure and cholesterol — but a new study suggests that these factors, combined with proteins in the blood, could help forecast people's risk of heart attack and stroke decades in advance.

The new study, published Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal JAMA Network Open, took a broad view of the factors that spike the risk of stroke or heart attack. The researchers found that warning signs for these conditions can be seen in patients' health data up to 30 years before they happen.

The researchers say their work shows that some understudied biomarkers — measurable signals in the blood — could be useful tools in anticipating later conditions.

"We did know that there are some well-established risk factors that are related to heart disease, for example, blood pressure, cholesterol," said study co-author Dorien Kimenai, an epidemiologist at the University of Edinburgh. But "nobody really has looked at the patterns of these risk factors prior to when these people are getting cardiovascular events — not systematically."

For the new study, the scientists tracked data patterns from a diverse group of nearly 114,000 healthy people over 34 years. Their data spanned four long-term health studies conducted in the U.S., U.K., and Norway. At the end of the study period, the researchers divided data from participants who were still healthy at that juncture from those who had experienced heart attacks or strokes and either died or survived the events.

But even at the study's outset, these two groups' blood pressure and cholesterol data showed a clear divergence.

"We did see that, even three decades before, already, that these patterns were different," said Kimenai. That suggests, she added, that the difference between the two groups likely began even earlier than that.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also divided their participants by sex and age, finding that men and women experienced different trajectories in their cardiovascular disease risk over time. Women, on average, started with lower blood pressure than men in middle age, but that switched later in life.

"It shows that the age effect is as important as the sex differences," Kimenai said. In short, both factors need to be taken into account.

Dr. Sintip Pattanakuhar, a clinician scientist at the University of Strathclyde in Scotland who was not involved in the study, said that while these risk factors can't be modified in the way blood pressure or cholesterol can, age and sex could be incorporated into personalized screening programs for cardiovascular risk.

During a stroke, the brain's blood supply is blocked or a blood vessel bleeds inside the organ. This reduces the blood and oxygen supply in certain parts of the brain, driving tissue damage and death.

The team also looked at the trajectories of biomarker proteins that circulate in the bloodstream and are linked to cardiovascular disease. These include cardiac troponin and N-terminal pro B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP), which are released by damaged heart muscle tissue and used to diagnose a heart attack. They also included C-reactive protein, a liver-borne molecule that signals rising inflammation in the body.

Differences in cardiac troponin and C-reactive protein were visible in people who would go on to have a heart attack or stroke up to 30 years before they happened. For NT-proBNP, the differences emerged about 10 years before.

That said, Kimenai cautioned that the biomarker data came from fewer participants than the full study cohort, so these results bear further confirmation.

Dr. Deepak Bhatt, director of the Mount Sinai Fuster Heart Hospital in New York, said the study's blood pressure and cholesterol data confirmed what cardiologists had long suspected about these risk factors: that these modifiable factors predict cardiovascular disease. Bhatt, who was not involved in the study, added that the biomarker data in this study built on other studies that have also shown that cardiovascular events can be predicted years before they happen.

"What this adds is that it's actually predicting events decades before," he said.

The study's clearest message was that people should get their cardiovascular risk factors checked early, Kimenai said.

"When you're 40 years old, get your risk assessments and your blood pressure measured," she said. "Because these are the things you can change. If you've then been identified as having hypertension, then you can get those drugs that are very effective and safe and efficient to alter the pattern."

However, while the value of checking blood pressure and cholesterol is well established, Kimenai and Bhatt agreed that the clinical value of the biomarker data was less clear at this stage. Bhatt said that he might advise a patient with high blood pressure to start medication and cut out salt, for example, but the way forward for someone with an elevated biomarker reading is less clear for now.

"Ideally, more work will be done" to see whether panels of biomarkers, perhaps combined with tools that measure genetic risk, could flag patients at very high risk of having heart attacks and strokes and should be treated differently than a patient with lower risk, Bhatt suggested. "That's sort of the missing piece of the Holy Grail of prevention."

#6105. The 7 Best Pocket Knives for Everyday Tasks and Outdoor Adventures

Our favorite folders, flippers, and automatics from Benchmade, CRKT, Case, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Cutting tools were likely some of the earliest tools fashioned by our prehistoric ancestors, so it’s perhaps surprising that knives are still one of the most popular tools in an age of 3D printers and electric scooters.

Modern EDC pocket knives have evolved quite a way beyond stone shards, with a bewildering variety of blade steels, blade shapes, opening and locking mechanisms as well as diverse aesthetics ranging from tactical to minimalist to outdoorsy.

This guide focuses on functional folding knives with (mostly) approachable price tags that you’ll want to use every day, not place under glass. I test dozens of knives each year, and I’ve chosen my favorites below only from the knives I’ve personally used.

The Iridium is one of Kershaw’s most popular releases and for good reason. It’s priced modestly with a secure bar lock-out, easy one-handed opening and closing, and it just looks cool. It’s also the sweet spot for most people in terms of size, weight, and style. Not ultralight (just over three ounces), the 6061-T6’s aluminum handle and slim profile keep it barely noticeable in your pocket.

When testing, I found the 4.5-inch length was great for my medium-sized hands and shouldn’t be too big or small for any hands—or jobs. Kershaw offers low- and mid-priced production knives made in China, but they follow up with high-quality control in their Oregon facilities and consistently deliver designs that just work.

At the core of the Iridium series is a secure, Benchmade-style crossbar lock, and while there are models that veer into Benchmade prices, many models, including the original, can be had for less than $100.

The Iridium is easy to use—opening with a smooth action, activated by the thumb stud opener. Though it’s not spring-assisted, the blade flicks open fast without resistance. Closing is similarly smooth—just pull down on the crossbar lock and close with a finger, or hold upright and let the blade fall shut. I usually prefer the satisfying speed of a flipper, but the smooth action of the Iridium’s thumb stud opening rivals the Benchmade Bugout’s, and it quickly grew on me.

The D2 steel used in the original, which offers decent edge retention and durability, is common in lower-cost knives but can rust if you abuse it. A compromise option: Go with the black oxide-coated D2 blade which keeps all but the cutting edge sealed off from rust. The look on all these versions of the Iridium matches the modern design features, and the only drawback of how smooth and slick the knife looks is that it’s not the best for operating in wet or muddy conditions where grip could become an issue.

Coast is one of several Oregon-based knife manufacturers (the company also sells a wide range of flashlights and headlamps) to offer a range of budget-friendly folding pocket knives. My favorite from their lineup is the fairly small but robust Contra, which has an all-metal build and a lifetime warranty despite the low cost. The wharncliffe blade, made from a softer 7CR17 steel, dulls faster than high-end steels but has the benefit of being easy to sharpen at home.

The wharncliffe blade gives you the utility of a box cutter blade but much more versatility as you retain a decent point for puncturing tasks, and I’ve come to prefer it for everyday carry over more traditional drop point shapes. Coast adds durability to its budget steel with a black oxide coating that I found doesn’t scratch easily. The knife is a full stainless-steel build with a good-looking stonewash finish on the handle which integrates the frame lock system.

The flipper opening is fast and satisfying for knife fidgeters but it’s usually safer to employ a two-handed closure. Given the overseas production and ultra-low sticker price, this pocket knife’s durability could be a potential concern, but I’ve used mine roughly near-daily for more than a year and haven’t broken or chipped the blade. It still looks new.

Benchmade is an American knife brand based in Oregon with a loyal following for its premium production pocket knives. Known for lightweight designs, modern materials, and innovation, the brand has produced many favorites—but my top pick is the Benchmade 535 Bugout.

To me, the Bugout captures what Benchmade does best: an ultralight folder that’s still strong, well-built, and made with high-quality steel (and the same holds true with the Benchmade 533 Mini Bugout). Some might argue the Benchmade Osborne 940 is the brand’s most iconic knife, but I reach for the Bugout every time—especially for hunting, camping, backpacking, or backcountry skiing, where weight matters.

The design is modern without feeling overly tactical. It’s streamlined with a simple profile and a practical drop-point blade. The textured Grivory scales—glass-reinforced plastic—keep weight incredibly low while maintaining rigidity.

At under two ounces and just 0.42 inches thick, the Bugout is barely noticeable in a pocket, making it ideal for long outdoor trips. For those who don’t like the Grivory feel, there are versions with aluminum or carbon-fiber scales and a range of steel options.

Operation is another highlight. Benchmade’s Axis Lock uses a spring-loaded crossbar that allows easy one-handed opening and closing from either hand while keeping fingers out of the blade path. The mechanism is simple, strong, and easy to maintain—I even built one myself at the Benchmade factory and found it intuitive without instructions.

In terms of cutting performance, my Bugouts arrived razor-sharp out of the box. I prefer the standard S30V steel because it balances edge retention with easier sharpening in the field, though higher-end options like S90V are available if you want longer-lasting sharpness. S30V is also tough and corrosion-resistant, which suits hard outdoor use.

Benchmade’s lifetime warranty and sharpening service add real long-term value. The Bugout isn’t cheap, but with its reliability, ultralight design, and customization options, it’s easy to recommend—especially for outdoor enthusiasts or anyone wanting a high-quality everyday carry knife.

Case is one of the original American knife brands still standing and, unlike many of their competitors that have shipped production to China, most of Case’s knives are still designed and produced in Bradford, Pennsylvania.

Whether or not that matters to you, Case makes great knives, and while they sell a lot of nostalgic designs unchanged for a century, the Kinzua is one of their modern EDC offerings that departs from the Case aesthetic with an all-metal build, flipper action, sharp lines, and a tanto blade.

The satin-finished S35VN steel blade is a good compromise of hardness and edge durability while still being fairly easy to sharpen at home. It also has a lightly weathered look that should hide abuse well. One note is that, while extremely sturdy, the all-metal frame-lock design is pretty stiff to close out of the box.

Releasing the frame lock requires some force and closing requires a few moves. With a little practice I was able to comfortably operate it one-handed, but folks with smaller or weaker hands may not feel the same.

The Bugout is one of our favorite Benchmade folders, and we recommend it above as our Best Lightweight pocket knife. But the brand’s new Bugout Vapyr variant is different enough to warrant its own place on the podium. The most noticeable difference is the width. The original Bugout is featherlight at two ounces, but the Vapyr gets that down to 1.72 ounces and shrinks the width by 3 mm, which is very obvious in the hand.

It’s impressive engineering, but practically, it takes a knife that was barely noticeable in the pocket and makes it borderline undetectable. It costs $375—nearly double the regular Bugout—so this is for folks with fewer budget constraints who are willing to spend for the lightest, thinnest folder that doesn’t compromise on utility and durability.

Part of that price jump can be chalked up to Benchmade swapping in MagnaCut steel for the S30V in the baseline Bugout. S30V is already a great blade steel with high corrosion resistance and incredible edge retention, and Benchmade has come to be known for using it. But MagnaCut is a step above on both metrics.

The other big change is the Axis lock, which remains functionally the same but swaps in a new stepped slide in place of the longstanding metal button. It’s a minor swap that first-time Benchmade buyers likely won’t even notice. But having used Axis locks for years, I much prefer the new slide.

There’s a subtle internal change from an omega spring to a tension spring. It didn’t feel different when I used it side by side with the original Bugout, but Benchmade says the tension springs have a longer lifespan. It’s worth noting that while better durability is welcome considering the price tag, all Benchmade knives have a lifetime warranty (and lifetime sharpening service) if a spring were to fail.

One drawback from the original Bugout is that, at least with the Bugout Vapyr I tested, the pivot is much tighter and requires more force to open. You can open a Bugout one of two ways. One, you can use the thumb stud to spin the blade out into the locked-open position. Alternatively, you can pull the Axis lock open and flick the blade open. This second option requires a touch of timing and gets harder with the Vapyr’s tighter pivot, though I didn’t find the thumb stud actuation any more challenging in the Vapyr.

I’ve been looking for a good automatic pocket knife for years, and the CRKT Twist Tighe Automatic is the only one that I’ve found that doesn't feel like a novelty knife. It’s compact, lightweight, fun to use, and practical enough for everyday carry while still delivering the fun factor that draws many people to automatic knives in the first place.

Automatics, often called switchblades, are popular with knife enthusiasts because they’re inherently fidget-friendly. The Twist Tighe is an out-the-front (OTF) automatic, meaning the blade deploys straight out of the front of the handle. Besides being undeniably cool, I find the operation safer than many folding knives because it’s harder to accidentally place your fingers in the blade’s path when opening and closing.

The highlight is its smooth double-action mechanism. Sliding the spine button forward fires the blade; pulling it back retracts it. Many automatics I’ve tried are either stiff or inconsistent, but the Twist Tighe feels smooth and reliable even after repeated use. That ease of operation also makes it surprisingly approachable for people who aren’t experienced with knives.

The design comes from Canadian knife designer Brian Tighe, and the handle’s raised spiral grooves are a distinctive touch fans of his work will recognize. In the all-black configuration, the knife looks sleek and slightly dramatic without becoming impractical. My version features a tanto blade with a black titanium nitride finish, while other configurations of the Twist Tighe have double-edged blades and more colorful scale options.

Size and weight are also big differences from other automatics. At just 1.6 ounces with a 2.65-inch blade and about a 4-inch closed length, it’s remarkably small for an OTF knife and easy to carry daily. However, people with large hands may find it a bit compact.

Overall, the Twist Tighe combines premium materials like CPM MagnaCut steel with one of the smoothest actions I’ve experienced. If you’re looking for a compact, high-quality OTF automatic for everyday carry, it’s an excellent choice.

The CRKT Minimalist Nessmuk combines the classic look of an outdoor blade with everyday convenience—plus there are several carry options for its sheath. It’s also surprisingly affordable for the build quality, priced at well under $100, with 12C27 stainless steel that keeps the cost down while providing corrosion resistance and easy sharpening.

Another thing in its favor is its versatility beyond hunting season. Thanks to its broad belly, it excels at slicing food, carving wood, breaking down cardboard, and cutting cordage.

With three deep finger choils in the G10 handle, it remained comfortable in hand while I tested it, and the textured scales provided better grip than many larger knives with smoother handles. That may not be the case for folks with larger hands, however, considering the size of the handle. Still, for most people, it’s an excellent choice for a fixed blade that can handle general tasks.

Testing and reviewing knives is a mostly subjective affair, despite all the ink spilled over steel hardness and the trade-offs between edge retention and durability. And with that in mind, I should highlight that these selections are made by one person and thus subject to my personal biases when it comes to pocket knives.

While I’ve developed many idiosyncratic preferences over more than a decade of knife reviewing and 40 years plus of knife-using, the big one is that I am a knife user before a knife enthusiast. I can appreciate a “cool” knife design as much as any other knife nut that owns hundreds of knives, but I’m partial to folding designs that work well, fit my hand, and make my life easier in their role as an essential daily use tool.

We update this guide multiple times throughout the year, and I’m constantly testing new pocket knives to look for new models that are worthy enough to unseat the favorites—and I don’t do that lightly. Year-round testing allows for longer-term use instead of a couple days of fidgeting with a blade and writing up a review. Most of the pocket knives featured here have been in my pocket on and off for months if not years, tackling everyday tasks as well as seasonal jobs such as butchering an elk or deer (if I’m lucky). We’ve included knives from the downright cheap to prohibitively expensive, but all the knives featured are ones we feel deliver good value considering the price tier.

As a baseline for any new knife, I check the factory edge for sharpness, look for corrosion resistance with a saltwater bath and air drying, and (when feasible) disassemble the knife to better understand the lock and open/close mechanisms. After beating up a knife for a while, I also sharpen the blade with stones with an angle guide to find out just how easy it is to return the blade to sharp. One of my favorite tests is handing a knife to friends and strangers to see how regular people react to opening and closing one for the first time, since I spend more time with knives than most.

Choosing blade steel is where knife geeks can get into the weeds. There are trade-offs, though, with any type of steel. Broadly speaking, if you go with a softer steel it means the blade may get dull more easily but it's also easier to sharpen. Harder types of steel hold an edge longer but might be trickier for novices to sharpen at home.

Steel characteristics also affect how prone a blade will be to rusting; however, most decent modern pocket knives use a steel that’s rust-resistant enough that it won't require lots of special care. Almost all knives’ product pages will list the type of steel used, and if they don’t, it’s likely a budget knife. If you can’t find the steel online, check knife marketplace sites such as BladeHQ for the make and model.

Here are the highlights for some of the more common pocket knife steel types:

Handle material is also an important choice. Wood is less common these days and less durable than steel or lighter, more durable synthetic materials like G10 and carbon fiber. Still, you may prefer the feel and look of wood despite the drawbacks. Steel is strong and durable but adds weight which can be a positive or a negative depending on how you use the knife and what you prefer hanging on your pocket.

A knife’s dimensions and weight affect the fit in your hand and ease of use. In general, bigger hands won’t like tiny knives and vice versa, but how and where you carry a knife impact your preferences for size and weight. If you’re an office executive, you may not want an oversized, obvious blade for daily carry, while working on a farm or in the trades, you might prefer a bigger, burlier blade to stand up to prying tasks and day-to-day abuse.

The action of a pocket knife can play an outsized role in your appreciation for it. I routinely test a lot of folding knives and find the knives I reach for most often are ones that are the most (subjectively) satisfying—and that I can easily operate one-handed when my off hand is busy doing something else. If you carry it long enough, you’ll get proficient with most any knife, but each of these common mechanisms has its strengths and weaknesses to consider.

In the previous century, secure locking mechanisms weren’t common, but today they’re expected if not universal. Classic knives, such as Case’s beloved Stockman and Victorinox’s iconic Swiss Army Knife, use slip joints, which hold the blade open but don’t truly lock. Because of the increased safety of a locking blade, I recommend choosing a pocket knife with some kind of a locking mechanism. If you are comfortable with a slip joint or other non-locking blade and enjoy the style, by all means, buy one. Note that your choice of lock typically dictates how you close the knife, so this will have a major impact on how easy it is to operate.

If cost is a major factor for you, it will quickly narrow the range of options. Knives can range in cost from just a few dollars to hundreds or even thousands for custom and limited edition options from celebrated knifemakers. Most people, however, will be looking at what are called “production knives”—models that are mass-produced, usually in a factory instead of by hand from individual knifemakers. While these blades can still run up to $500 or so, the range is much tighter as the cost to produce is lower.

Knives for less than about $20 will usually feature softer, cheaper steels and inexpensive handles. These knives may have less quality control than pricier models, but you can still get a decent knife from an established manufacturer any day of the week for less than $50. For example, the cheapest knife I recommend costs about $25.

Choosing a pocket knife with harder carbon steel will usually push the price closer to $100 or more. Go past that $100 price point, and you’re paying for specific designs, brand names, and other personal preferences, but you’ll start to see diminishing returns as far as raw functionality.

In the United States, carrying most pocket knives won’t break any laws. But each state has its own rules that might restrict the specific pocket knives you can legally carry. Many states have prohibitions on certain automatic knives, on blade length, and even on whether or not you can carry certain knives concealed.

The American Knife and Tool Institute has a helpful state-by-state guide to knife laws you can consult. Traveling abroad brings an even wider range of regulations, as some countries such as Austria have almost no restrictions while Norway (despite a rich knifemaking heritage) has an outright ban on carrying knives in urban areas.

Possibly. First, not all pocket knives are the same. The legal definition of pocket knives may vary across states and at the federal level which can impact shipment and receipt.

Most states also have some kind of restrictions on what knives you can carry on your person. Even in wild west Colorado where I live, it is illegal to carry a blade longer than 3.5 inches “concealed” which would include “in your pocket.” In New York state where I grew up, switchblades are illegal and you must be a U.S. citizen to even own a knife, but there are no concealed carry restrictions. Check your state laws here.

Outside of local laws, consider how a knife fits in your hand. A knife that feels tiny and awkward to someone with large hands might be perfect for someone else. If you’re not already a regular pocket knife carrier, stop into an outdoors store where you can handle a wide range of knives and see what feels good. Most people will feel comfortable with blades in the 2.5- to 3-inch range, though folks with larger hands may want something bigger.

I’ll start with a caution—that you may not want a surgically sharp pocket knife. Because I use my pocket knife so frequently and casually, I don’t like to be as cautious as you have to be with an ultra-sharp blade.

I experimented with carrying a replaceable blade knife for a few months and I ended up giving myself several minor but annoying slices. That said, any knife will eventually require sharpening. Most pocket knives have a fairly obtuse 20-degree or higher blade angle, which makes them less challenging to sharpen yourself.

Knife sharpening is a skill that’s not easy to master (learn how here), but there are tools available to help. While whetstone sharpening is soothing in a Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance sort of way, you probably already have a pull-through sharpener somewhere (check kitchen drawers).

These sharpeners aren’t the perfect sharpening solution, but they’re relatively idiot-proof and good enough to perk up your blade. If all of this sounds like something you’ll never bother with, there are lots of mail-in sharpening services such as The Sharp Brothers, who will professionally sharpen your blades for a fee. Also, many manufacturers offer similar services. Benchmade, for example, has a LifeSharp program that gives you free sharpening for any Benchmade knife. Some manufacturers such as Kershaw also offer blade replacement (often for a fee) if you’ve broken or otherwise damaged your blade beyond repair.

This is both a surprisingly common and difficult-to-answer question. Obviously personal budget comes into play, but so do your preferences. Despite considering myself a pocket knife enthusiast, I carried a cheap pocket knife from Walmart for years that cost me literally $1. The company raised the price to $2 at some point. Those knives would rust at the hinge, but they did the trick and were great for putting in my checked luggage. I wouldn’t worry about losing it at my destination and wouldn’t cry if the TSA took it.

While I can’t recommend buying $2 knives in good conscience for most circumstances, quality options such as the Coast Contra recommended above can be had for under $20. If you’re new to knives, start out with something cheaper, definitely under $50, until you develop strong opinions about the pocket knife you prefer.

Rachel is the Deputy Editor of Reviews for Hearst's Enthusiast and Wellness Group where she supports Popular Mechanics, Runner's World, and Best Products. Her background is in service journalism and earlier in her career she worked as a daily newspaper reporter and book editor. She spent more than a decade as a staff editor and writer at TripAdvisor and Penguin Random House and her byline has appeared in Time Out New York, the New York Daily News, and New York Magazine. Outside of work, Rachel can be found planning her next trip, visiting museums and galleries, and walking her wirehaired dachshund in Central Park.

Live Science spoke with astrophysicist Erin Macdonald about her role as a science adviser for 'Star Trek' and other Hollywood movies.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

From gravitational waves to time travel, science has always been at the heart of "Star Trek". While the franchise has never shied away from imagining the impossible, much of its appeal comes from making strange situations seem believable.

That's where the role of a science adviser comes in. It's not necessarily about making sure everything is scientifically accurate, but understanding the science well enough to know where creative liberties can be taken and how to make them come alive on screen.

Erin Macdonald knows this balance all-too-well. After studying general relativity and gravitational waves for her doctorate and spending years working at Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), Macdonald shifted gears and became a science advisor for six "Star Trek" series, including the "Discovery" franchise, as well as a variety of other television and film projects. Live Science spoke with Macdonald about how she brings the world of "Star Trek" to life, and her job's biggest pitfalls.

Erin Macdonald is an award-winning writer, science communicator, producer, and science advisor. She is most well-known for her advising work on 'Star Trek' and has played her own character across multiple iterations of the franchise. As a science communicator she has also appeared on NPR, BBC, CBS, and StarTalk Live.

KHC: How did you end up getting into the field of science advising?

EM: After I got my Ph.D. and did a little bit of research, I realized academia and that world just weren't really for me. So I went into engineering, but I really missed teaching and being able to engage with students. I was trying to find more opportunities to do public science communication. I'm a big sci-fi nerd, so I started going to sci-fi conventions and giving solo panels and workshops that were basically, "Here's the physics behind faster-than-light travel," and "Here's all the physics in 'Star Trek'."

This article is part of a series called "Science Behind the Camera" which focuses on the role of science advisors. From helping to create engaging stories to set design and script rewrites, these experts shape some of the most compelling narratives on screen.

Through that particular talk and just life happening, I met a lot of people on the convention circuit. I decided I wanted to go to L.A. I learned that science advising was a job, so I moved out there, still working as an engineer.

CBS and "Star Trek" got wind of my talks, and they invited me to give presentations at their official licensed "Star Trek" events. That's how I got on their radar. A couple of years later, we were in a world where there were a lot of 'Star Trek' shows being produced, and they were looking for a science adviser for "Star Trek: Discovery". [Editor's Note: "Star Trek: Discovery" ran for five seasons (65 episodes) from Sept. 2017, to May 2024 on CBS] That went well, and they brought me on as an in-house science adviser.

KHC: You've now advised on how many shows?

EM: Well, six "Star Trek" shows, but I'm starting to lose track of the films and other shows I've been called into for either one-off things or bigger jobs. It's been a great experience.

I think a lot of being successful in L.A. and Hollywood is that every job is an audition for your next job. You work on one show, everyone goes their separate ways and works on new shows, and if they know someone they might want to bring in, they'll give you a call. I've been very lucky in that regard.

KHC: What does the day-to-day look like for a science adviser?

EM: All the jobs I've done are different. When I get pulled in to talk to someone about a new project, it could be almost anything.

The biggest role, and the one I enjoy the most, is being brought in when a show is just getting off the ground and the writers' room is being established. They'll bring me in to sit in that writers' room and help contribute to the ideas and stories as they're being developed. If questions come up in real time, I can help answer them. That's the most ideal scenario for being a science adviser because you can get ahead of any issues as plots are starting to be developed.

A lot of the time, when you're doing something wild like that, I'll just say, "Great, don't explain it. Do your thing. Try not to science it."

But it can also look like being handed production scripts. Basically, they've gone through the whole process, they're nearing the point where they're going to start filming, and they're like, "Hey, can you check this for us?"

That can be a blessing and a curse because it's a little less work, but then you can't course-correct as much if there are big plot problems. You have to find a way to work with the story and try to get the science as accurate as possible. In that scenario, it can end up being, "Don't explain it. Take these lines out. You're getting yourself in trouble. Leave everything else."

The last kind of job, and one I've had a lot of colleagues do, is set design. They'll be brought in when they're building sets or doing post-production and want to make sure what's on screen looks science-y.

The best example I can give is someone writing all the equations on "The Big Bang Theory". All those whiteboards you see? That's a scientist coming in to write all of that.

Science advisors may help with set design, such as writing the equations on the whiteboards in CBS's popular show "The Big Bang Theory."

I worked on a show called "Good American Family" on Hulu. It's not a science show at all, but they had a kid who was really interested in physics. I went in and wrote all the equations and talked to the actor about how to say the things he was going to be saying.

The process can vary greatly. Even within "Star Trek", my relationship has been different from show to show. That's an exciting part of it, but I think people can see that it's a very varied position.

KHC: Out of all your 7 years of experience in science advising, is there a particular scene, moment, or script you're especially proud of?

EM: There are certainly ones that are really close to my heart. I'll give a couple of examples.

One was the season two finale of "Star Trek: Lower Decks." I wasn't brought in until season two, At the end, the showrunner was basically like, "Hey, I have this vision, but we need to build the 'Star Trek' science around it."

He just had a scene in his mind and wanted to build the story. We came up with this great story about an asteroid belt with a lot of charged particles that disrupted the [protective] shields. There was a lot of good technobabble in there, too. It was really fun. Watching that episode, it just feels like a really authentic "Star Trek" episode because of all the science in it. I'm really proud that I was able to contribute to that.

If you spend your time just criticizing the science in films and TV, this is not the job for you.

Another one that stands out to me is the musical episode of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds". That was one of the first times the show was taking one of these big swings. The show is kind of known for doing all these big swings now, but that was one of the first. A lot of the time, when you're doing something wild like that, I'll just say, "Great, don't explain it. Do your thing. Try not to science it."

But they pushed back on me and said, "No, no, no. We need a science explanation."

We really worked together and came up with a detailed science explanation. What I'm really proud of is that they created that ready room scene [Editor's note: a ready room scene is a dramatic sequence set usually in a command office before a major battle or mission] where Spock explains everything that's happening. It's probably one of the longest ready room scenes we've had in "Star Trek". It's like, "And then this, and then this, and this is why, and this is why, and this is why, and this is what we need to do."

It's goofy, but there was a lot of science put into that episode, which was a really fun process.

KHC: I would be remiss if I didn't bring up the creation of Dr. Erin. How did that character come about, and how have you felt about the impact of the character?

EM: It's really funny. The character of Dr. Erin has now shown up in multiple series, video games, and comic books, which delights me.

Macdonald's influence as a science adviser resulted in the creation of the character Dr. Erin, based on Macdonald herself.

The origin of it started on "Star Trek: Prodigy". It was a "Star Trek" show aimed at children. They wanted me to come in not just to help make sure the science was right, but also to do more traditional science communication and help create a character who was a kid who wanted to be a scientist and talk about what that process is like. That's the character of Rok-Tahk, and she's adorable.

As they were reaching the end of season one, the kids were going to Starfleet Academy, and the showrunners were like, "She has to meet Dr. Erin. She is who she is because of Erin." That was just one of the greatest honors. It was a quick, one-line mention, not even named in the episode.

KHC: Is there anything you wish you could change from your perspective?

EM: Yeah, there are a few that haunt me a little bit.

There are some shows where I was really involved, we meshed well together, and I helped with the story. There are very few things I would change. But then there are other shows where I'm just given the script at the 11th hour. Plot-wise, would I have suggested something different? Yes. But it was too late to course-correct.

One really good example was in "Star Trek: Discovery". They had an episode where they were trying to ride gravitational waves out of a nebula, as one does. They had that ready room explainer moment, and they were showing the gravitational waves as literal sine waves, like the ocean waves you think of. I was working with the visual effects team, and I pushed back. I said, "Really, these are compression waves." You could still make an argument that they were going to ride them out, but it's more like how sound waves move. They're compression waves.

To their credit, they animated that and put it in the scene. But as people were watching it, they felt that the way we were talking about it versus what we were seeing just wasn't working. It was pulling people out of the scene, so they had to revert back.

It was funny because when that aired, I had three or four former gravitational wave colleagues who were like, "Erin, you had one job."

Gravitational waves are compression waves, like sound waves, as opposed to sine waves.

Another quick example was an episode in season one of "Strange New Worlds" where Spock says, "We're being pulled into the black hole."

That's one of those moments where it's technically not correct. You fall into black holes. It's a very public misconception that I try to fight back against a lot. Black holes aren't hoovering things up. It's just deep gravity. But in the context of the scene, Spock is being very condescending and talking down to La'an, so he's simplifying the language for the public. I can sort of get away with that.

KHC: Is there anything else you think our readers should know about science advising?

EM: I meet a lot of people who, delicately or not, say, "I could do your job. I'd be a great science adviser." I think what's made me successful in science advising is that I take a very "yes, and" attitude.

I'm a fan first and foremost. If you spend your time just criticizing the science in films and TV, this is not the job for you. You need to work with the stories you're given, and you need to understand the mission.

There's a quick anecdote. I worked on another film called "Space Cadet," which is a stoner comedy on Amazon, and they were having a really hard time finding a science adviser because everyone was trashing the script. It's ridiculous, goofy, and fun. They were like, "Look, we just want someone who makes sure the NASA people know what NASA people would say. That's it."

The job isn't for everyone. Storytelling comes first.

Editor's note: This interview has been edited and shortened for length and clarity.

#6103. Trump says no Iran deal needed after conflict drove GOP’s midterm losses

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance salute during a Wednesday ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery in honor of Veterans Day. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

President Donald Trump on Thursday shut down his administration’s on-again-off-again talks with Iran, saying he would not seek a deal to formally end the nine-month-old conflict with Tehran.

The possible end of the pursuit of a diplomatic solution came nine days after Trump and congressional Republicans suffered massive losses in the midterm elections. House Democrats will have more than 250 seats come January, and Senate Democrats will have at least 55 seats in the Senate — with Alaska’s competitive race still uncalled.

Polls leading up to Election Day and since have shown that a majority of voters, and a sizeable chunk of Trump’s Republican base, felt the Iran conflict was a mistake.

Vice President JD Vance penned a lengthy social media post the day after the election, blaming, in large part, the Iran war for the coast-to-coast Democratic victories. Some GOP lawmakers have also called for an end to the conflict, which drove up fuel and other commodity prices.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote the morning after the GOP wipeout. "The president himself said so last night."

Trump has said that he agrees with Vance’s assessment but that if he had to decide again whether to join Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in striking Iranian targets, he would reach the same conclusion. On Monday, he told reporters that the Iran war "militarily is effectively over."

Vance had been Trump’s designated top negotiator in the talks with Iran’s remaining leaders, but the president said Thursday on social media that he had ordered his second-in-command to instead “focus his complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S.”

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” he added. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!"

The situation along the Strait of Hormuz remains contested and dangerous for commercial vessels, including ones that deliver a large amount of the world’s oil products. Iranian officials contend that they control most of the key waterway.

Trump, Vance and other administration officials have said in recent weeks that they were open to continuing talks with Iran, while criticizing Tehran's negotiating tactics. Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also is Trump’s national security adviser, told reporters that Iran's latest demands were unreasonable.

Trump’s announcement Thursday could represent his latest way to try assuaging GOP voters, including members of his “Make America Great Again” base. A Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted after the midterms and released Tuesday showed that a majority of Republicans (51 percent) want Congress to pass legislation that would end the Iran conflict. Overall, 71 percent of Americans would support such a bill, the survey found.

The conflict was front-and-center during the midterms campaign.

Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, who lost the Senate race in Michigan to Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, called for the Iran conflict to end "quickly."

“Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down," Rogers said in one campaign ad.

On Capitol Hill, GOP lawmakers have tried giving Trump cover, while raising some concerns about high gas prices and questioning whether the president and his team have a viable exit strategy.

As the midterms campaign hit the homestretch in late September, two Iowa Republicans in tight races, Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, voted with Democrats on a measure to end the conflict.

“With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” Nunn, an Air Force veteran, wrote on social media. “I will not support another open-ended war.”

Nunn and Miller-Meeks both lost their seats last week, despite breaking with the president over the war.

Trump’s declaration this week of a military end to the Iran war came more than seven years after he offered some foreshadowing during a June 25, 2019, exchange with this CQ Roll Call reporter in the Oval Office.

Asked that day what his exit strategy would be if war ever broke out with Iran, he said: “You’re not going to need an exit strategy. I don’t do exit strategies.”

We've found the stargazing deals worth your money this Black Friday at retailers like Amazon and B&H, including some of our favorite models that we've personally tried and tested.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Black Friday is here once again, and if you've been waiting for the prices to drop before buying your next telescope, smart telescope or binoculars — this could be the time to pull the trigger.

But as we all know by now, retailers use these sales as a sneaky way to inflate their prices before the sale starts, so in many instances, their "sale" price is actually the same as it was before they put the price up. So how can you be sure that the price you're seeing is truly a deal?

Well, we keep track of prices throughout the year, and use tools to check when they fluctuate. We know whether something is a genuine deal, and, crucially, whether the product is actually worth buying in the first place.

We've searched the web for the best genuine deals on the telescopes, smart telescopes and binoculars that we have actually tested ourselves, so you can be confident you're actually saving money and not getting played by capitalism.

Telescopes give you breathtaking views of the moon and planets.

A great beginner telescope that the whole family can enjoy. This 4.5-inch Newtonian reflector comes with a 20mm eyepiece for scanning across the sky and a 10mm eyepiece for detailed views of the moon or spotting Saturn's rings.

The EQ mount requires a bit of tinkering, but it's a useful skill to have once you've figured it out, as it makes tracking objects across the sky easier than an Alt-Az mount.

This model usually retails for $319.99, so a $40 saving on a telescope of this quality is pretty good.

We've reviewed a smaller telescope in the AstroMaster range, the Celestron AstroMaster LT 70AZ, and our optics writer owns the Celestron AstroMaster 130EQ, which has a slightly larger aperture.

The Celestron StarSense Explorer range is great for anyone who wants to start stargazing but doesn't yet have any knowledge of the night sky, and this model in particular is a good option if you want to invest in something you can grow with.

The setup is a straightforward Alt-Azimuth mount, and you can use the smartphone dock to navigate your way around the sky with the guidance of the StarSense app.

It has a 5.1-inch (130mm) aperture and comes with 25mm and 10mm eyepieces, giving you beautiful views of the moon, Saturn's rings, Jupiter's cloud bands and wide views of some deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy and the Orion Nebula.

The price tends to fluctuate throughout the year, although on average it sits between $420 and $450. However, it's been the full $499.95 since September, so this price is definitely worth taking advantage of.

Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ review

Although it's very close in aperture to the StarSense DX 130AZ we listed above, the differences in optical design and focal length offer a different observing experience.

This model is the better choice if you want higher-magnification observations of the Moon and planets, thanks to its 1,250mm focal length. It also has a much shorter optical tube, so it's more compact and easier to transport. The Schmidt-Cassegrain design is more complex to manufacture than a Newtonian reflector, hence the difference in price between the two.

It was $579.99 throughout most of the year, rising to $589.99 in August, which it has been ever since.

Smart telescopes will locate, track and stack images for you, making astrophotography easier than ever.

Granted, it's not the biggest saving ever, and it isn't listed specifically as a Black Friday deal, but you can save $35 on the ZWO Seestar S30 Pro at Amazon. This is the cheapest we've seen it since its release, and it typically stays at the $699 RRP.

It's an incredible way to get into astrophotography, even for complete beginners. It's an all-in-one system that automatically locates, tracks and stacks images of stunning deep-space objects for you. It's compact and portable, with a quick and easy setup and produces beautiful 4K images.

The smallest and most affordable smart telescope on the market is now even more affordable (but still the same size).

It only produces 2K images, which is still plenty for sharing with friends and family or on social media. In practice, it just means you'll be more limited when it comes to cropping.

It's been $419 since August, and this Black Friday deal is the cheapest we've seen it since its release.

If you're a more advanced user and have been waiting to upgrade, this is one of the best chances you'll get. You can now save a whopping $1,000 on the Unistellar eVscope 2 right now.

It has an aperture of 114mm and a 450mm focal length, making it ideal for deep-sky imaging of even faint and small objects. And the electronic Nikon-produced eyepiece adds an immersive element to the experience, rather than viewing everything on your screen.

Read our full Unistellar eVscope 2 review

Another fantastic saving from Unistellar, and the Odyssey Pro doesn't have as much reach as the eVscope 2, meaning it works better on wider objects.

The Odyssey Pro has an 85mm aperture with a 320mm focal length, which is still plenty to get stunning views of galaxies and nebulas. It also has a Nikon eyepiece that shows you how your image is doing as it's stacking — which is beneficial if you're not connected to the app.

Vaonis describes the Vespera 3 as the "most affordable premium smart telescope on the market," and judging from its specs, we'd be inclined to agree.

It has a new apochromatic quadruplet design that eliminates chromatic aberration and field curvature across the entire frame, excellent clarity even under city skies, a massive 11 hours of battery life and built-in multi-night capture.

It has a 50mm aperture and 245mm focal length, with a native image resolution of 8.3MP, or up to 24MP with covalENS mosaic mode.

If you liked the sound of the Vespera 3 but wanted something a little more powerful, the Vespera Pro 2 is $500 off for Black Friday.

It offers a higher resolution of 12.5MP native and 50MP mosaic, has more internal storage (225GB vs 115GB), and comes with a carbon fiber tripod (as opposed to aluminum) and a hard case, which are perhaps more suited for traveling to dark skies.

We've been testing it out over the past few weeks and are incredibly impressed. The images we've taken of the moon, for example, are breathtaking. The Vespera Pro 2 is currently the highest resolution smart telescope on the market.

Big astronomy binoculars are more portable than a telescope, making them ideal for camping trips and spontaneous stargazing outings.

If you're looking for a pair of binoculars you can take anywhere, with excellent optical quality and edge-to-edge sharpness, the Celestron Regal ED 10x42 is an excellent investment.

The ED glass eliminates chromatic aberration, and it has field-flattening lenses to correct curvature, resulting in sharp, bright and detailed images with basically no defects. Perfect for observing the moon and stars with excellent clarity.

We have seen them cheaper at the start of the year, but over the summer they've been $379, so this price is worth taking advantage of.

Read our full Celestron Regal ED 10x42 review

If birdwatching is more your thing, the 8x42 variant is also in the Black Friday sale.

If the Regal ED is a little out of budget, the Nature DX ED range is an excellent, more affordable alternative that still offers great image quality.

This variant in particular is ideal for birdwatching, thanks to the 8x magnification, and the ED glass is ideal for following birds in flight. Plus, you can enjoy views of the moon and get a closer look at the stars.

We have reviewed the Celestron Nature DX ED 10x42 variant, although this model isn't included in the Black Friday deals.

Big astronomy binoculars are a must for any sky-lover, and the Celestron SkyMaster Pro ED 15x70 are perfect for getting detailed views of the moon, stars and even spotting Jupiter's moons.

They typically fluctuate between $279 and $309, and although they aren't currently listed as a Black Friday offer, the $25 you can apply at checkout makes them the same price as the variant without ED glass. Personally, we'd always buy the pair with ED glass.

Read our full Celestron SkyMaster Pro ED 15x70 review

With a massive 20x magnification and 80mm objective lenses, these are serious skywatching binoculars that provide stunning detail in the night sky. They're perfect for close-up views of the moon and stars, and you can also spot Jupiter's moons and some of the brighter deep-sky objects.

This is the cheapest we've seen them since June, and they tend to fluctuate between around $270 and $319.

Read our full Celestron SkyMaster Pro 20x80 review

The Pro ED version is also discounted, although not labelled as a Black Friday deal. There's a $30 coupon you can apply at checkout to get them down to $319.97.

Black Friday technically starts at 00:00 AM on Friday, November 27, 2026, running all weekend until 23:59 on Monday, November 30, 2026, which is known as Cyber Monday. However, many retailers have been running early Black Friday deals for the past couple of weeks.

Pretty much all of them! We've sourced these deals from our trusted retailers, including Amazon, B&H Photo, Best Buy, Walmart and others.

We've done the legwork for you. We've checked the price history of all these deals to make sure you aren't being fooled, and we have personally tried and tested all the products we have recommended.
