#6101. The 8 Best Trail Cameras for Hunting, Wildlife Watching, and Even Home Security

These expert-tested trail cams help hunters and wildlife watchers capture what happens off-grid.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons. Even if you’re not heading into the woods to hunt, it’s one of the most interesting times of year for observing wild animals. Whitetail deer, elk, bears, and other animals are becoming much more active due to seasonal mating periods while waterfowl and other birds migrate for the winter.

The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem. If you’re considering a trail camera that uses a cellular network to send photos and videos directly to your smartphone, the good news is these have gotten even easier to use.

While the trail cam experience improves every year, the cost of many units is more than $100, and cellular models require recurring data plan charges, making it trickier to assess value. Images from game cameras are better than ever, even in budget models, and apps add software features often.

Sorting out what matters most to you and how you plan to use your trail cameras can be a challenge, so we explain what to look for along with sharing our top recommendations selected from year-round testing of dozens of cameras evaluated side-by-side.

The Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 replaces the Reveal Pro 3.0 camera, our previous pick for Best Overall. Released this summer, the Pro 4.0 version keeps what made the 3.0 great and improves on it in two key areas: image quality and battery life. Reveal has one of the best apps in the space, with tons of settings and features to tweak your setup and manage your cameras and images. Updates to these basics are big usability improvements that demanding trail camera users will notice.

Cameras going dead in the field is a major gripe for users of these gadgets. You have to physically go and replace batteries, which adds hassle and cost to your experience. I tend to place cameras in early summer and let them run for several months until my hunting season starts. The problem is that active cameras can run through eight to 12 AA batteries in a month depending on the model and your camera settings.

Tactacam has tackled this issue in a few ways with the Pro 4.0 release. The brand told me it audited everything about camera operation that drained the battery and then made small tweaks to reduce power demands anywhere it could.

Tactacam has also developed sold separately R5 and R10 lithium battery packs that replace previous battery add-ons, which have the notable benefit of swapping into the same form factor as the AA battery tray, so they don’t add bulk to the camera.

Image quality in the Reveal cameras has always been solid, but the company took a unique approach to dealing with the challenge of getting both crisp day and night images by installing separate sensors for each. Photographers know that night images require different gear and settings than daylight shooting, so the split makes sense. The early returns from a month of testing confirm that the quality of both day and night is much improved.

The rest of this flagship Reveal camera is impressive, carrying over from the Pro 3.0 and now-discontinued Ultra camera. The Reveal lineup now has just two similar cameras: the Pro 4.0 and the X 4.0. The Reveal X 4.0 is basically the Pro 4.0 without a built-in display screen, which saves $30 and is a great option if you don’t value the screen for aiming and reviewing images at the device.

As mentioned, the robust app gives you remote control over everything including photo and video capture settings, transmission frequency, night image flash, trigger delays, and more. You’re also able to launch a live stream to follow up on interesting images, but there’s an additional subscription cost and it will drain the battery quickly. There’s also built-in GPS that shows the location of your camera on a map within the app—essential if you’ve forgotten where you placed it or if it’s stolen.

Cell-connected trail cameras are handy, but if you’re low on funds or trying to run a multitude of cameras, paying $150 and up per camera gets pricey fast. Spypoint’s Flex M2 trail camera keeps both the upfront purchase cost and recurring subscription fees reasonable. Spypoint even has a free data plan that gives you 100 images per month if you want to avoid subscription fees altogether. (The Flex M2 doesn’t have onboard memory, nor does it ship with an SD card, so you’ll have to spend at least another $20 per camera for a high-speed SD card.)

Despite the low price, the camera’s 32-megapixel photos and 1080p video are clear and well-exposed. The Flex M2 displays lower-resolution images in the app but you can request full-resolution images when you want more detail. This is beneficial because it keeps data demands low and shows up in the battery usage as well. After a month in the field, the eight AA batteries I was using displayed in the app at “High” strength.

Additionally, I appreciated that this camera is compact since I’m usually hauling my cameras several miles into the backcountry in a pack. If you want to run this camera year-round, I’d consider picking up the $60 five-watt solar panel add-on, which has a built-in battery and should allow you to leave the Flex M2 up indefinitely.

I was impressed with the overall experience with the Flex M2, but the highlight here is the cost to purchase and run this camera. Yes, you’ll need to pay up for video or a higher quota of images, but this is a great option if you want the excitement of getting trail camera images on your phone without the annoyance of yet another recurring subscription fee on your credit card.

There are two significant recurring costs with a cellular trail camera: the data plan and batteries. Connected cameras can chew through batteries, which can add up, especially since you’ll want to use more expensive lithium batteries if you can. Sehmua’s 4G Solar Trail Camera comes with rechargeable batteries and a solar panel, which allows the camera to run indefinitely given adequate sun exposure.

The camera itself has a fast trigger and 2K photo and video that can be saved to an SD card, or to cloud storage for an additional cost. The app, which is a little clunky and can be confusing due to some quirky menus and word choices, works with images that show up quickly and reliably.

Notably, even though this is a 4G cellular-connected camera, you can still use the camera to record to the SD card if you decide not to pay for one of the data plans. This is another sneaky way this camera provides solid value for its low price point.

The best way to cut down on battery costs for your trail cameras is running solar panels. While many cameras have the option to run on solar, it’s often an additional upfront cost. The new 2026 Moultrie Edge 4 Solar trail camera has it all smartly packaged together in an integrated unit that costs less than some standalone cameras.

Setting up solar often requires separate mounting as well as hauling out lots of separate pieces and cables to be connected. The Edge 4 Solar just straps to a tree as a single unit, ready to run indefinitely. The camera comes with a rechargeable lithium-ion battery powered by the panel, which enables you to place a camera and leave it running as long as you need. Having the solar panel integrated is convenient and compact, but you’ll need to choose spots wisely to ensure both good captures and sun exposure.

Beyond the solar power setup, the Edge 4 is a solid trail camera with crisp 40-megapixel photos and 1080p video. The app is polished and makes setup and use hassle-free even if you’re not particularly tech-savvy. The subscription plans are in line with the industry average, ranging from $8.99 to $22.99. The lowest-tier plan offers more than most other companies’ $5 plans (1,000 images and 10 videos) and the most expensive plan offers unlimited images and 50 videos and discounts steeply to $7.99 per month for each additional camera.

The convenience of cell-connected trail cameras is undeniable, but if you’re burned out on subscription charges and don’t mind checking your cameras manually, you can save a significant amount on your trail camera setup. The WOSPORTS Trail Camera is a budget option with impressive image quality and low one-time cost. The camera doesn’t ship with the required eight AA batteries, but it does come with an SD card.

This compact G600 records imagery to an SD card and lasts longer since it doesn’t use batteries communicating over cellular networks. You’ll have to walk into your hunting zone to swap cards, but the purchase price is a fraction of the lifetime cost of buying and operating a modern cell-connected setup.

The 56-megapixel images and 4K video aren’t Planet Earth–level quality, but I was still more than satisfied with the pictures and videos I got. I don’t put too much stock in megapixel numbers as a true measure of trail camera image quality because these numbers are mostly inflated with software enhancements. That said, the images and videos from the WOSPORTS camera were sharp enough for clear identification of details.

The Defend by Reveal 360 is not your traditional trail camera—it’s closer to a home security camera that’s designed to work anywhere. Ring and other doorbell cameras usually rely on WiFi for connectivity, which makes them impractical more than about 50 yards from your router. The Defend 360 uses cellular networks instead so you can place this camera anywhere with a decent cell signal.

In the field, the Defend 360’s biggest advantage is motion. Most trail cams are fixed in place, but this one adds remote pan-and-tilt control, allowing you to reposition the camera from your phone. Its 355-degree pan and 75-degree tilt effectively eliminate blind spots when combined with the wide-angle lens.

Like a regular trail camera, motion detection triggers photos only to conserve battery and data. A 1080p live view can be activated on demand when you need a closer live look. That approach makes sense for remote monitoring, though it feels different if you’re used to continuous video feeds from home security cameras.

A rechargeable battery and included solar panel allow for long-term deployment with minimal maintenance. Setup is straightforward via the app, and the camera automatically connects to the strongest available carrier via eSIM.

There are a few downsides. Night footage is serviceable but not amazing, and like most cellular cameras, it requires a subscription plan to unlock full functionality. Still, if your goal is reliable, wide-area monitoring in remote locations, the Defend 360 delivers better coverage and control than standard trail cameras.

A lifetime warranty usually isn’t reason enough alone to buy a product, but in the world of electronics generally and with trail cameras specifically, it’s unheard of and fairly compelling.

With Yellowstone.ai’s Y2 Camera and Solar Bundle, your upfront cost is on the higher side at $250, but the solar panel and rechargeable battery mean no recurring battery costs. You’ll also save on gas and time, since this is a cell-connected camera, and there’s no need to visit the camera unless you want to move it.

Compared to the big-name trail camera apps, the app is not quite as polished, but over several months of testing, I did not experience any of the quirks and bugs I’ve experienced with some trail cam apps from overseas companies (Yellowstone.ai is U.S.-based).

The image and video quality isn’t quite as sharp as the top tier of the cameras I’ve tested like the Reveal Pro 4.0 or Moultrie Edge 4 Solar, but it’s by no means unacceptable. I was impressed by features such as built-in GPS, automatic cell network selection, and remote settings adjustments.

The solar bundle comes with the panel, Y2 camera, and two rechargeable battery packs. If you want to keep the upfront cost down, the camera alone is half the price at $125.

No matter how great your trail camera placement, it’s easy for cameras to miss animals. This is exacerbated in big open areas such as wetlands or crop fields where it can be hard to know precisely where animals might appear.

Muddy’s Trifecta 180 is built to minimize these misses. Three motion sensors and a rotating camera capture wide-angle 180-degree images. This is the perfect camera for the edge of large agricultural fields where animals could appear anywhere and often turn up in groups that can be hard to capture in a single image. You have the option for the camera to stitch together impressive panorama images (though they’re harder to appreciate on a phone screen) or the option to capture single-zone images like a regular trail camera would.

The downside of this impressive device is that it seemed to use more battery power than usual, likely attributable to the camera’s need to move and the usual drains of taking and transmitting images. If you’re planning on running it long-term, I’d consider picking up the solar panel accessory with integrated battery.

I’ve assembled my choices in this guide based on years of firsthand testing, and I continue testing new trail cam options every season to keep up with the constant rollout of new features and improvements. For decades, I’ve been hanging trail cameras with professional hunters and friends to capture wallowing elk, nursing moose, and scavenging bears on camera.

Historically, I’ve preferred inexpensive, simple cameras that I monitor manually, which keeps my trail camera budget in check, but as connected cameras have gotten more reliable and affordable, I’ve shifted to using cell cams almost exclusively. I hunt in three different states as well as in spots several hours from my home in Colorado, which makes manually checking all my cameras nearly impossible. I still employ “manual” cameras around my property where pulling memory cards frequently isn’t a pain.

One of the main divisions in the trail camera market is whether your trail camera connects to a cellular network, which, if it does, is what allows you to wirelessly send images over great distances. Connected models are so common now that AT&T and Verizon offer monthly service plans that often come bundled with the camera.

This connectivity means that you don’t have to physically visit your camera to check out the imagery it has captured—a benefit that’s most tangible when cameras are placed in far-flung hunting spots, but less valuable if you’re using the camera closer to your house. The cellular connection also makes the cameras easier to operate since most cell-connected cameras can be controlled via your smartphone through apps. These allow you to use remote-control camera settings to switch between photo and video modes, adjust camera sensitivity, and check battery levels.

Networked cameras are addictive to use because they can provide instant, or at least frequent, gratification from your camera(s). However, there’s usually a recurring data plan cost in addition to setup complexity. Bottom line: Be sure you really need the connectivity. There also may be legal restrictions on wirelessly connected cameras that limit how you can use them. Be sure to double-check your state’s regulations before buying.

All trail cameras store images locally on the device, whether or not they have the ability to transmit them wirelessly. More often than not, that storage comes in the form of an SD or micro SD card, which you can remove to download your photos. Cameras with wireless support, however, now often feature an internal hard drive, which stores data more reliably, since you no longer need to physically “pull cards” to collect your footage.

If you’re planning to only use a networked camera, I recommend choosing a camera with internal memory. The No. 1 source of problems I’ve had over the years of testing dozens of different trail cameras and helping others set up many more is memory cards. These plastic chip-like cards are fragile, easy to lose, and can be formatted incorrectly. Even when there’s nothing wrong with a card, cheaper SD cards with slower transfer speeds can cause errors when processing larger images and videos.

The only advantage of having a camera with removable memory is if you want to use the camera without a data plan. This is required for the increasingly rare non-networked cameras, but even connected cameras can be used manually if they have physical cards. Some cameras with internal memory also have an optional SD card slot, such as the Reveal Pro 3.0, which gives you the option to expand storage capacity and use the camera without paying for a data plan.

This might seem like a minor detail, but given that many people want their trail camera to capture their subjects without alerting those subjects to the camera’s presence, the camera’s exterior color can be a critical factor. Since a majority of trail cameras are marketed to hunters and are intended to be used outdoors, these devices generally come in solid earth tones or camouflage patterns.

If you’re a hunter, you probably already have a good sense of what patterns are most appropriate for your area. If not, snap some photos of the trunks of the trees where you intend to mount the camera; then compare them to the patterns on the cameras you’re considering.

Cameron Shrum, avid bowhunter and co-owner of C&K Archery in Frisco, Colorado, says, “People will get a good deal on a camera and not realize how important it is to have [it] match [their] habitat. The goal is to get pictures of animals without them knowing they are being watched, and when something is out of place, game animals have a tendency to figure it out.”

As a professional photographer and videographer, the first thing you need to know about judging the quality of a camera is that there is no single metric that easily tells you which camera will record more clearly. At a glance, checking specs like the number of megapixels in a camera’s sensor gives you a decent clue as to what you can expect.

Ultimately, the best way to gauge the quality of a trail camera is with your eyes. Take a minute to look at sample photos posted by customers on retailers such as Amazon, which give you a practical way to evaluate images taken under natural conditions.

Trail cameras rarely take print-worthy shots, but that isn’t what they’re for. If you’re just patterning animals, image quality isn’t as crucial as simply detecting them. Trophy hunters trying to identify certain calibers of animals or monitor a specific animal across multiple cameras will want to be more picky about image quality and clarity.

Even if you don’t need great fidelity, a better image makes using trail cams more useful and rewarding. I’ve come to appreciate having modern trail cameras that deliver clear images and 4K videos over the crude, fuzzy work of older, lo-fi models.

I recommend using only lithium batteries in trail cameras. Especially with cheaper cameras, I’ve found that regular alkaline batteries don’t provide enough voltage for the IR flash, and many times a trail camera may not record video with underpowered batteries (alkaline batteries start decreasing in voltage as soon as you start using them). Lithium batteries deliver higher voltage consistently, and they work better in the cold.

If you’re setting up a cellular trail cam, make sure you check signal strength in the area. If you have a camera that offers an app or website (as many now do) that lets you view images on your smartphone, try triggering the camera and see if you receive the notification and image.

Since trail cameras are often left alone for days, weeks, or even months at a time, setting them up properly is important. Shrum recommends testing your trail camera before you walk away. “Have it snap a few pictures with you walking by and then review them. Sometimes you may not have the right angle; it may be too high or too low. Try to set the height and angle to capture the game in the center of the camera’s view.”

Trail cameras are usually strapped to a tree and most come packaged with a long strap for this purpose. If you’re placing a camera somewhere without convenient trees for the angle you want, look into a camera stand or even a tripod. Most trail cameras have a standard tripod plate mount (¼-20) and stands or stakes are available from most manufacturers.

A common spot to place cameras is along well-traveled game trails. A tip I picked up watching champion archer Levi Morgan put up cameras on one of his hunting leases: rather than pointing the camera down a trail where it’s likely to be in the line-of-sight of animals as they walk it, put the camera off-trail between 10 and 30 feet away perpendicular to the trail. This will usually give you broadside images of animals instead of head-on and puts the camera in their periphery.

Once you’ve tested your placement (and image transmission for connected cameras) by viewing a test photo on the app or the camera itself, scan the camera’s field of view for new-growth vegetation. Plants and tree branches can result in a near-constant stream of false triggers on a windy day. I like to place any plants or branches I cut behind the camera for a bit of concealment, making sure they can’t blow in front of the camera.

Since trail cams are motion-activated, a fast trigger seems important. You don’t want an animal to pass by the camera before you get a photo, right? In my experience, the real problem is taking the photo too quickly, which results in seeing just the nose of a slow-moving deer. Still, many brands tout their fast trigger speeds as if they solve an important problem.

“It’s kind of a BS spec, frankly,” Gregg Farrell, vice president of marketing for Tactacam Reveal, told me. “The goal is to capture the animal in the center of the frame and our cameras do that through the operating system working with the [motion] sensor.”

Most trail cameras have listed trigger speeds around a half second, which can work well, but are often too quick if implemented poorly. I almost always switch my cameras to shoot a multishot burst, if available, to give the camera more opportunities to grab a well-framed shot. Keep in mind, though, that this will double or triple the number of images you receive, so it may not be a solution if you’re using a cell-connected camera and trying to save with a limited-data plan.

Some cameras have detection delay settings that let you set a period of time after an image is captured before it’ll take another. This can cut down on look-alike images if an animal is hanging around in the detection area, especially if you’ve enabled a multishot mode.

Connected trail cameras make scouting convenient, but they come with hidden costs. Almost all cellular trail cameras require a monthly data plan to cover the cost of cloud storage and image transmission.

Many companies tack on extra fees for features such as live streaming, which eat up a lot of data and cost the companies money with their network provider partners. Like sitting at a blackjack table, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of scouting and click your way to hundreds of dollars in recurring monthly charges. You can review the details of each company’s data plans before you buy and decide what features you want to use in advance. You can save money on a camera if you decide you don’t need all the latest features and avoid the temptation of activating those extra charges in the process.

Common game animals such as whitetail deer and elk tend to settle into routines during the summer months which often persist into early fall. The change of seasons and seasonal mating windows will help throw routine out the window in the fall, but if you can identify high-traffic areas in the spring and early summer, that will likely continue all summer.

The best practices for finding a good spot and setting up the camera properly are the same in any season. Spring in some ways makes it easier to identify animal travel patterns since the ground is often wet and recent activity is more obvious. Hike your zone and look for fresh signs to identify intersections, pinch points, and frequently visited locations. If you’re able to access your cameras easily and often, use the early season to experiment with different locations for a few weeks and try new spots you hadn’t considered before that show promise based on animal signs. Half the fun of placing these cameras is finding that perfect location and image framing that yields a ton of exciting wildlife images.

There are plenty of things that can trigger a trail camera other than the type(s) of animals you’re looking to capture, including squirrels, lights, and vegetation moving in the wind. “False triggers,” as we call them, are not only disappointing, but waste storage and burn through your data plan. It’s hard to eliminate them completely, but there are lots of ways to minimize them.

The most important is proper camera setup. Once you’ve got it framed up the way you want and have a successful test image, look for branches and weeds in the frame, primarily in the foreground. A single goldenrod stalk or pine bough can burn through a month’s data allotment on a windy day, so take your time to clear the immediate area in front of your camera.

You can’t always clear cut in front of a camera, so if you find you’re still getting more false triggers than you’d like, adjust the camera’s trigger sensitivity down. Many cameras only offer high or low, but if you have a more finely graded adjustment such as the 1 through 10 sensitivity settings on the Reveal Pro 3.0, adjust slowly down until you stop getting false triggers so you don’t overcorrect and miss animals.

Some cameras also use recognition software to reject images that appear to be empty. Moultrie’s Edge cameras allow you to only accept motion triggers in selected zones of an image, effectively blocking triggers from, for example, a corner of a detection zone with moving tree branches.

Most states have some sort of regulation with the use of trail cameras, especially when used on public land and as they relate to hunting activities. Arizona, where game animals tend to congregate around limited water sources, banned trail cameras for hunting statewide in 2021. Colorado, where I live, has few restrictions on trail camera use before your hunting season begins, but limits employing them while you’re actively hunting.

Using trail cameras on your own private property doesn’t usually involve too many restrictions, but be sure to check the regulations from your state’s wildlife management organization to confirm, as private land practices can still be regulated through the hunting codes since wildlife are considered a shared public resource.

There are so many options for security cameras dedicated to home use, and because of that, most of the time it makes more sense to just buy a security camera from a brand that specializes in that application, such as Ring or Google Nest.

These products generally have superior apps and software to hunt-focused trail cameras. Since they're designed for home use, they effortlessly connect to your home WiFi network, don’t require a data subscription, and will have features trail cameras won’t such as two-way communication.

That said, if you already own trail cameras and don’t need specific features, most trail cameras can serve a security purpose. The best trail cameras to employ for security are the newer “live” trail cameras that transmit imagery instantly via cell networks and notify you on your phone when the camera has been triggered.

Another option is WiFi-enabled trail cameras that can connect to your phone without a cellular network to transmit images. However, these cameras don’t usually transmit if you’re not within range of the camera (i.e., at home), so they’re limited to general monitoring rather than real-time notification when you’re away.

Jamie, Senior Reviews Editor, joined the Hearst Enthusiast Group in 2021. She has covered technology and consumer lifestyle gadgets since 1995—and shared her expertise in print, digital, and in broadcast originating the role of The Gizmo Girl for ESPN’s Cold Pizza. She has written about, tested, and reviewed everything from turkey fryers to high-definition TVs. Her byline has appeared in TWICE, Sound & Vision, Consumer Reports, and many others. In her free time, Jamie is in a yoga class, searching for the perfect matcha latte, or walking the boards.

Live Science asked its readers what type of archaeological find they'd want to discover.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

From people's backyards to famous excavation sites, archaeological discoveries found the world over give clues about the cultures and lives of ancient peoples. For instance, the discovery of 1,200-year-old pennies in Denmark revealed that the Vikings melted down silver from the Muslim world, while an excavation of a 2,800-year-old tomb with sacrificed horses in Siberia revealed ties to the nomadic Scythians.

Other archaeological discoveries are important due to their historical significance or extraordinary preservation. For example, the 40,000-year-old "Lion Man" statuette was carved by humans in what is now Germany during the last ice age, and it may be the earliest known evidence of religious belief in the world.

Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide clues about mysterious and long-lost languages, such as the Linear A writing system from the ancient Minoans of Crete. Other texts, like the Rosetta stone, helped crack the code of Egyptian hieroglyphics, allowing researchers to better understand this ancient culture.

Each type of archaeological discovery unearths something new about the ancient world. This week, Live Science polled its readers on which of these types of findings they'd most like to uncover.

Over 290 readers weighed in, with 69% choosing that they'd like to discover an ancient text "that helps decipher a language."

The comments also reflected this trend, with one reader writing: "The interpretation of a newly deciphered language can lead to the discovery of other things like tombs and documents, as was the case with the Rosetta stone. Once Egyptologists could read hieroglyphs, they could discover other information which helped them in their research and digs."

Other readers highlighted the importance of finding ancient weapons, which 4% of participants voted for. As one commenter wrote: "War has always been responsible for where people gather and settle down together. Weapons therefore can reveal the ebb and flow of people across the countries, which for many years never existed. This therefore reveals a lot about the specific development in many different areas and ultimately perhaps as to why we actually live where we do."

In a similar vein, one commenter wished that they could "discover Attila's grave site, since no one has found [it] as of today."

Another reader reflected on the importance of finding ancient burial sites, writing: "I think that tombs are the most valuable finds in archaeology."

Do you agree or disagree with these readers? What would you most like to find? Let us know in the comments!

Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

When alpha-gal syndrome first emerged, it was a baffling medical mystery. Today, diagnoses are rising, yet much about this potentially life-threatening condition remains unexplained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sandra Tiguila, an adventurous eater, enjoyed a bison sausage breakfast sandwich while dining out in August of 2025. On the drive home, she noticed a rash appearing on her wrist. The burning sensation spread to her arms and legs, making it nearly impossible to sleep. In the days to come, she tried creams, pills, injections; nothing helped.

Ten days later, Tiguila ate out again, ordering a steak. When her face swelled up, her boyfriend drove her to the emergency room. A doctor tested her for diseases carried by ticks. Tiguila, who lives in Carbondale, Illinois, had been bitten twice that June.

Tiguila went home and the next morning, as she was drinking coffee with her usual supplement of bovine collagen for joint, hair and nail health, the test results came in. She had developed a red meat allergy that’s activated by tick bites. "I immediately dumped that coffee down the sink," says Tiguila. She started avoiding all mammal products — the main way to manage this rising and occasionally life-threatening allergy.

Known as alpha-gal syndrome, the condition arises when the immune system reacts to a certain sugar molecule, called alpha-gal, that’s found in red meat. Symptoms range from a mild rash or stomach upset to anaphylactic shock; in 2025, alpha-gal syndrome was blamed for the death of an otherwise healthy 47-year-old man. The syndrome has only recently been characterized and is still not fully understood. Though Tiguila, who is a nurse, was aware of the allergy, she says she still failed to connect her rash to her meaty meals and earlier tick bites.

As ticks have spread northward, so too have alpha-gal diagnoses. Up to 450,000 people in the United States may have been affected since 2010, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates.

"It's emerging as one of the top adult-onset food allergies," says Onyinye Iweala, an allergist and immunologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

Sandra Tiguila, who acquired alpha-gal syndrome after being bitten by ticks, frequently walks her dogs in this wooded area near her home in Carbondale, Illinois.

Allergies are often mysterious, but this one is extra weird. "Alpha-gal follows none of the rules that I was taught in training about how a food allergy behaves," says Maya Jerath, an allergist and immunologist at Washington University in St. Louis and one of Tiguila's physicians. For example, unlike with other food allergies, where reactions are immediate, alpha-gal symptoms often show up hours after eating meat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

And, strangely, the allergy often arises after a tick bite. In the early 2000s, Jerath recalls, Australian allergist and clinician Sheryl van Nunen first shared tales on the scientific-conference circuit of patients with a delayed allergic reaction to red meat after tick bites. "Nobody believed her," Jerath says.

The eventual unraveling of the mystery would happen on the other side of the world, where immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, unaware of van Nunen's findings, was pursuing two parallel projects in his lab at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville. In one, his group was collecting blood samples from people claiming weird meat sensitivities. In the other, they were investigating patients' strange reactions to the cancer drug cetuximab. It would take both projects to crack the case, recalls Scott Commins, an allergist who was then part of the lab and now works at the University of North Carolina.

First, the cancer strand. Cetuximab is a drug designed to stick to cancer cells and block their overzealous growth. It was first approved to treat colorectal cancer in 2004, but as its testing and use spread, an odd pattern appeared. In the Southeastern United States, more than one in five patients had allergic reactions to the drug — hives, difficulty breathing and even anaphylaxis.

It took about a year and a half, Commins recalls, but Platts-Mills' group found the culprit. People who reacted badly to cetuximab, they discovered, had blood loaded with proteins called IgE antibodies. When activated inappropriately, IgE causes allergies. The cancer patients with the allergic reactions to cetuximab had IgE antibodies that were reacting specifically to the sugar alpha-gal, the researchers reported in 2008.

Now, humans (and many other primates) don't make alpha-gal. But most mammals do. It's one of several sugars that cells attach to proteins to regulate their final structure and function. And cetuximab, like many drugs, is manufactured in lab-grown mouse cells. These cells had attached alpha-gal molecules to the cetuximab. That's what triggered the allergic reactions in the cancer patients.

But it only happened in some of the people taking the drug. Why them? And why only in the Southeastern United States?

The next clues came from the lab's other work, on meat sensitivities. This puzzle, of course, also involved exposure to tissues from non-primate mammals — so the researchers hypothesized that this allergy had the same cause as the drug reactions. Sure enough, they found that people with meat sensitivity also had elevated IgE antibodies to alpha-gal, causing a "novel and severe food allergy," the team reported in 2009.

The allergy is bizarre for several reasons. There's the delay that van Nunen had noticed. And food allergies are typically triggered by protein: egg protein, nut protein, etc. While some carbohydrates have been linked to mild allergies, a sugar causing such severe reactions was unheard of, says Jeffrey Wilson, an allergist and immunologist at UVA Health in Charlottesville, Virginia.

Plus, food allergies were supposed to be all-or-nothing: A person allergic to peanuts will always react to peanuts. Not so with alpha-gal. For example, some people react to meat alone; others might be bothered by dairy or other mammal products, such as gelatin in cosmetics or medications.

It took several strands of evidence to determine that tick bites can trigger an allergic reaction to the alpha-gal sugar.

Because those products are common, people are exposed to alpha-gal all the time. The sugar can even be made by natural gut bacteria. In other words, most people have no problem with alpha-gal. Platts-Mills, Commins and colleagues were still missing an explanation for why only some people developed this odd sensitivity.

So Commins led a study of people with and without meat allergy to see what the allergic ones had in common. Might they have been exposed to some kind of fungus, or maybe a worm? No, and no.

Then, a key clue emerged from a colleague down the hall. He'd had the meat allergy and joined the study, but had been doing well, so he dared to eat a sausage. Big mistake: He had a bad reaction. Testing showed his alpha-gal IgE had risen to "freakishly high levels," Commins recalls.

The colleague also had itchy spots — from recent tick bites. That got the team thinking. Commins went back to his meat-sensitive subjects to ask if they'd had tick bites. Most of the nearly 200 people answered yes. The team then learned of van Nunen's work, published in 2009, bolstering confidence that they were on the right track. Everything pointed to a tick link: The regions where people had alpha-gal antibodies overlapped with the range of the lone star tick; people who got bitten developed more alpha-gal antibodies, and people with those antibodies often also had antibodies to other lone star tick proteins, the team reported in 2011.

Later, biologist Shahid Karim of the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg and colleagues found alpha-gal in lone star tick salivary glands. The final clincher implicating ticks came in 2023: Commins and collaborators at the CDC reported that people with alpha-gal syndrome were more than 11 times more likely to recall finding a tick on their body than those who didn't have the allergy.

Around the world, about a dozen tick species are now associated with alpha-gal allergy. In the United States, the lone star tick is the major player, and it's spreading northward, helped by warmer temperatures and exploding populations of deer that the tick feeds on.

Given the expanding health concerns, the CDC has pledged $10 million to support alpha-gal surveillance and awareness among health providers and the public. Scientists, meanwhile, have lingering questions about how the mysterious allergy works.

The pathway from tick bite to meat allergy remains murky. Commins, who hosts a podcast about alpha-gal syndrome, speculates that the body can treat alpha-gal as either something to tolerate or something to react to. The route of exposure seems to be key: Alpha-gal in the gut, from food or bacteria, seems to promote tolerance. But exposure via the skin is a great way to trigger an allergic reaction. That reaction can overshadow the tolerance, often temporarily, Commins says. This hypothesis fits some of the allergy's features: A strong reaction to the initial bite, or getting lots of bites, boosts risk. Fresh tick bites can also exacerbate or reactivate the sensitivity.

Tick bites can prime the body's immune system to perceive the alpha-gal sugar as a threat.

Researchers don't really know why certain ticks cause the allergy and others don’t. One possibility: Perhaps the lone star tick's taste for human blood, combined with, as Commins notes, its wickedly long skin-piercing mouthparts, underlie this species' proclivity to incite allergy.

Also puzzling: Some people get tick bites and don't develop the allergy, and some alpha-gal patients don't report any history of tick bites. Some people have high levels of IgE antibodies to alpha-gal but can enjoy cheeseburgers freely. Others are sensitive to meats but have low concentrations of the allergic IgE.

Karim, for his part, is trying to figure out what causes some tick victims' immune reactions to flip from alpha-gal tolerance to allergy. Some research suggests that blood type is a risk factor. Type B blood proteins contain a structure similar to the alpha-gal sugar, and this could promote tolerance, making people with type B or AB blood less likely to develop IgE antibodies to alpha-gal.

Another unresolved question is the odd symptom delay. Wilson speculates that it could be explained if the alpha-gal sugar is hooked to meat fats, rather than meat proteins. Fats take longer for the body to digest and transmit into the bloodstream, so only then would the alpha-gal sugar gain the notice of immune cells.

For some people, their elevated IgE levels will drop and the allergy will go away. In others, it lingers. And sometimes it seems to morph into a generalized disorder where people have allergy-like symptoms even when they avoid meat, says Iweala.

For now, there are no specific therapies for alpha-gal. Allergists can suggest antihistamines and offer EpiPens to thwart a reaction. Some prescribe Xolair (omalizumab), a general allergy treatment that can minimize symptoms if a person encounters alpha-gal. To avoid activating or exacerbating alpha-gal syndrome, the best approach is to avoid tick-ridden areas or use insect repellents like picaridin on skin and permethrin on clothing.

And Commins hopes to create a better treatment. It's known that an immune signaling molecule called IL-4 is key to the allergic response. He's in discussions with pharmaceutical companies to test a treatment that would interrupt this IL-4 messaging.

Better therapeutics would certainly be welcome. Alpha-gal syndrome can cause anxiety, since mammal-derived products are ubiquitous and hard to avoid. Tiguila, when she was first diagnosed, went into a label-checking frenzy; she almost threw a bag of prunes across the room because it contained a possibly mammal-derived additive.

A number of factors can influence whether a person will develop an allergy to the alpha-gal sugar.

After visiting the Washington University clinic and being advised to relax around foods that didn't bother her, Tiguila calmed down. She still enjoys the great outdoors but is careful to slather on insect repellent first.

She recently received more good news: In August of 2026, her blood tested negative for IgE antibodies against alpha-gal, suggesting that her allergy might be gone. Her physicians prescribed a reintroduction protocol they had developed for patients who hit this milestone. She started with an ounce of filet mignon, a low-fat cut, and amped up the exposure from there. "I've successfully returned many people to eating meat again," Jerath says. In one study, her protocol worked for all 19 participants.

Add Tiguila to that total: As of late September, she is back to her usual diet. "I'm very grateful to be cleared and not have to be so cautious," she says.

#6098. Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage declared winner of open House seat

Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, fifth from right, joins incoming members Thursday for their freshman class photo on the House steps outside the Capitol. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Paul LePage, the former Maine governor who once said he was “Donald Trump before Donald Trump,” is heading to Congress.

The Associated Press called the race for the open 2nd District on Thursday after the Maine Secretary of State’s office tabulated the votes under the state’s ranked choice voting system. LePage ended up ahead of Democratic state Auditor Matt Dunlap 50.8 percent to 49.2 percent.

Dunlap had already conceded the race to LePage, who will succeed retiring Democratic Rep. Jared Golden in the sprawling district, which includes much of Maine outside the Portland and Augusta areas.

“Paul LePage is already hard at work for the people of Maine attending Congressional orientation, meeting with national leaders, and making it clear the political parties need to work together for the American people,” Brent Littlefield, a senior adviser to LePage, said in a statement Thursday. “As Paul said, he will work with anyone, regardless of Party, to put Maine first.”

LePage’s win is a glimmer of good news for Republicans, who saw massive losses across the country in last week’s midterm elections. He is one of three Republicans, along with Texas’ Jace Yarbrough and Tennessee’s Brent Taylor, to have flipped a House seat, although Maine’s 2nd District is the only one of the three that wasn’t redrawn to favor the GOP.

LePage’s win also means that at least one Republican will continue to represent New England in Congress, taking up the mantle from Maine Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her own reelection bid last week.

Golden, who was first elected in 2018, had been a top Republican target throughout his time in Congress. But the lawmaker, known for bucking his party, proved difficult to unseat in the past two election cycles.

“I also know a thing or two about winning in tough circumstances. So, I know you have to tip your hat to Paul LePage for winning in the midst of this Blue Tsunami,” Golden said in a social media post last week.

Dunlap initially launched his campaign as a primary challenge to Golden in the fall of 2025, only for the congressman to announce his retirement a month later. Dunlap went on to win a four-way contest for the Democratic nomination.

Researchers might have identified the oldest male orca ever recorded after testing for radioactive traces of atomic bombs in the teeth of whales stranded in Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nuclear fallout has potentially revealed the oldest male orca ever recorded, scientists have found.

The radioactive residue, a result of bomb testing in previous decades, was preserved in the teeth of orcas (Orcinus orca) and sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) that washed up over the years in Scotland, according to a recent study.

"It gives us what we call a kind of bomb pulse," study first author Kieran Tierney, a research scientist at the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre, told Live Science.

Male orcas are thought to have a maximum lifespan of around 50 to 60 years. However, in the recent study, published Oct. 1 in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science, the radiocarbon signature identified in one stranded male suggested he had lived to more than 65 years old.

The research team noted that the radiocarbon data doesn't provide a precise age. However, that doesn't mean the estimate is implausible.

Maximum ages are notoriously difficult to measure in nature — researchers can't track every animal to see which individual lives longest in all species — and there isn't an extensive worldwide record of orca longevity.

"The age estimates we have from life history studies are only a few decades old and researchers have only looked at limited numbers of individuals from a few orca populations," said Erich Hoyt, co-chair of the IUCN Important Marine Mammal Area Specialist Group and author of "Orca: The Whale Called Killer" (Firefly Books, 2019). "It would not surprise me if male killer whales were sometimes living to age 65 and beyond," Hoyt, who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Orcas and sperm whales have banded growth layers in their teeth, which researchers believe form every year, like the rings in a tree trunk. To test this idea and learn more about the animals washing up in Scotland, the authors of the new study examined teeth from three orcas stranded between 1995 and 2016, and from two sperm whales stranded in the 1990s.

Researchers studied the tooth of an iconic male sperm whale named Moby, which stranded in 1997.

Atomic weapons testing, particularly during the middle of the 20th century, unleashed vast quantities of radioactive material, including radiocarbon, which subsequently entered the marine environment and is preserved in the teeth of cetaceans like sperm whales and orcas. Radiocarbon exists naturally in the atmosphere, but the detonation of these bombs significantly spiked environmental levels of this radioactive isotope, so by measuring levels of this compound, researchers could identify whether animals lived through the testing era.

Banded layers in the sperm whale teeth matched the atomic data, with the two whales estimated to have died in their 20s and 40s, respectively, suggesting that the layers formed annually at least in early- to mid-life. However, while the tooth layers and atomic age matched for one of the orcas — estimating the animal was in its early 20s — the other male's data didn't match at all, according to the study.

The oddball orca, named KW2, stranded in Uist, an island in western Scotland in 2015. The tooth analysis suggested that KW2 lived into his 50s, but the radiocarbon analysis suggested he was at least 65 when he died. Tierney speculated that either a cluster of layers appeared in the tooth as a single year, or new layers stopped forming in later years.

"We think that the tooth effectively ran out of space to put down any more layers," Tierney said.

The banded layers and atomic data also didn't match for the study's only female orca, named Lulu. In Lulu's case, she didn't have a clear bomb pulse signal, making comparisons difficult. The tooth layers suggested she was in her 30s when she died, while her radiocarbon signal was indicative of historic nuclear plant discharges in the Irish Sea in the latter half of the 20th century, which were carried to the Scottish west coast.

By looking at stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen in the tooth samples, the researchers identified traces of what the animals might have eaten. Lulu appears to have had a higher proportion of marine mammals in her diet than the males, which seemed to eat more fish, according to the study.

Orcas' diets vary across different populations, and Lulu's is likely tied to her community. She was part of Scotland's West Coast Community — a genetically distinct orca population on the brink of extinction — before she stranded in 2016. The West Coast Community is known to prey on other marine mammals.

Lulu was famous for being the last known female in the West Coast Community. The population hasn't produced any calves in the decades researchers have studied it. Now down to just two surviving males, the remaining bulls are expected to be the last of their kind.

While the West Coast Community's living bulls weren't part of the new study, they are thought to be more than 50 years old. This longevity, combined with the estimated age of KW2, raises tantalizing questions for future orca research.

Tierney noted that until now, orca studies have mostly focused on populations off the Pacific coast of North America. There, males have a mama's boy reputation; they're typically observed spending their entire lives with their mothers, with life expectancy dropping significantly after their mothers die. But if male orcas are living longer lives off Scotland, and the West Coast Community's bulls are getting by without their mothers' support, then it's possible they could be more independent than their North American Pacific counterparts.

"It looks like the killer whales around our shores maybe do something a little bit different," Tierney said.

Tierney, K. M., McGill, R. A. R., Brownlow, A., Sayle, K. L., Tripney, B. G., Dunbar, E., Newton, J., Terrapon, M., Doeschate, M. T. I. T., Davison, N. J., Timmons, Z., & Kitchener, A. C. (2026). Integrating radiocarbon and stable isotopes in odontocete teeth to reveal life histories. Frontiers in Marine Science, 13. https://doi.org/10.3389/fmars.2026.1934180

#6095. At the Races: Regional realignment

New England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, New England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.)

One Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged New England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”

#MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

Redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a new congressional map.

California contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Guv update: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

Senator Morrison?  Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

AOC’s future: Progressive activists have launched a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is New Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

Congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The New York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

How Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”

Song of the cycle: The New York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The New York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

If those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

#6094. Briggs and Riley Discount Codes | Black Friday 2026

I’ve often sung the praises of Briggs & Riley, and for good reason. Known for its dependable construction and chic design, the brand’s suitcases have proved to be one of my absolute, reliable travel companions. Take the Sympatico medium expandable spinner—it’s my go-to piece of checked luggage, a mainstay in my rotation for traveling across the globe. It’s logged serious miles with me, from rolling across the cobblestones of Florence to the sweeping landscapes of Montana without so much as a loose wheel. Even after getting lost for two weeks at JFK Airport, it returned to me without one scratch.

Briggs & Riley’s commitment to reliability traces back to its founding in 1993 by luggage industry veteran Richard Costa, when the brand made its name with an innovative design and a straightforward promise: a lifetime repair guarantee that covers damage even if an airline is responsible.

Of course, luggage built this well rarely comes cheaply. Many of the brand’s most popular pieces sit firmly in investment territory, at around $500 and above. That’s precisely why the occasional sale or promo code is worth noting: Ahead, the Briggs & Riley discounts and Black Friday promotions currently on our radar—so you can pick up one of our favorite travel companions for a little less.

If upgrading your travel gear is on the holiday shopping list, now is a good time to give your suitcase a little attention. Briggs & Riley is offering up to 30% off select luggage and travel bags in its Black Friday sale, while supplies last. There's more than a few tempting finds in the mix, including the Baseline Traveler Tote, now $149 (down from $235), a handy overnight bag with a slip-through back panel that slides over your suitcase handle; the Torq Domestic 22-inch Carry-On Spinner, reduced to $449 from $579; and the roomy Baseline Extra Large Expandable Spinner, now $799 instead of $1,025, with expandable packing capacity for longer trips. As an added bonus, orders over $399 also come with a free gift. Consider it a head start on your next getaway—and a nice little upgrade before the new year.

Briggs & Riley honors active-duty military members and veterans with 15% off full-price merchandise. This applies to the brand’s full lineup of checked luggage, carry-ons, and travel accessories—everything built to last a lifetime and backed by their famous lifetime repair guarantee. Verification is simple: confirm your military status through GovX, a secure platform for service members. Once approved, the discount can be applied at checkout.

For travelers looking to up their ante on an entire luggage set, the brand is offering stellar deals on some of their hottest selling collections. The Lifetime Set, for one, is $200 off and best for the essentials, with one large checked spinner, one compact checked luggage, and a durable carry-on. The Essentials Set is another fabulous option, with $100 off the chic Sympatico Essential 22" front pocket carry-on expandable spinner—plus, all the practical gear that fits inside of it: the matching compression packing cub set, a zippered laundry bag, two shoe bags, and an expandable essentials kit for any toiletries or smaller items in need of storage. You can find plenty of more where that came from on their Signature Luggage Sets page.

If you’ve traveled enough to know what makes a suitcase worth its weight, Briggs & Riley’s bestsellers speak for themselves. Travel accessories from the Sympatico Collection begin at $15 (for a personalized patch), with luggage starting at between $500–$600. Options now come in a one-of-a-kind, limited-edition Glossy Ruby, which turns heads with its bright, high-gloss finish while still standing up to serious wear. The TORQ Collection is all about hard-side durability and smart front pockets for keeping essentials close at hand.

One of the reasons travelers remain loyal to Briggs & Riley is the brand’s famously straightforward promise: its Simple as That lifetime guarantee. In practice, it means your suitcase is covered for life when it comes to repairs—even if the damage happens in transit and even if you purchased the bag elsewhere. Broken wheels, handles, or zippers can all be fixed, making the luggage feel more like a long-term travel companion than a short-term purchase.

Briggs & Riley offers free FedEx Ground shipping on all orders of $99 or more—which can easily be met with most suitcase purchases—within the contiguous United States. Eligible orders are automatically discounted at checkout, with no code required. #6092. Democrats mulling Iran war funding cutoff strategy

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., talks with reporters in the Capitol on Sept. 30. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A group of prominent Senate Democrats is pushing to use a must-pass spending bill to cut off funding for the Iran war, complicating the path toward a bipartisan deal for averting a partial government shutdown next month.

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Thursday he is working on legislative language ending the war that he wants attached to the next continuing resolution that is needed by Dec. 11, when current funding runs out.

“I know it’s going to be my main push,” he said. “I have to work with colleagues to try to find some language that works. And I’m not there yet, but I’ve told everybody that’s an opportunity.”

Democratic Sens. Michael Bennet of Colorado, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, Tammy Duckworth of Illinois and independent Bernie Sanders of Vermont released a statement Thursday that they would oppose any deal that does not include “language that restricts the Trump Administration from using appropriated funds to continue his war against Iran.”

“When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war,” the senators said. “It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve.”

It is unlikely that Republicans, who are in control of both chambers of Congress until January, not to mention the Oval Office beyond that, would agree to such a deal.

House Appropriations Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., said earlier this week that “a Republican Congress is not going to send bills to a Republican president that he's going to veto.”

While ending the war is a top priority of Democrats as they take back power in the new Congress, insisting on doing so this year could lead to a Christmas-time partial government shutdown. If a shutdown starts after Dec. 11, it’s possible it would still be ongoing when Democrats take control of both chambers in January.

But some Democrats appeared to still be weighing how quickly to push for a cutoff of war funding.

Senate Appropriations ranking member Patty Murray, D-Wash, said that whether or not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth remains in his job, “we’re still going to have language stopping this war.”

She was coy on whether that fight would take place on the anticipated continuing resolution in December or wait until next year when Democrats take back power, saying that lawmakers are “looking at all options.”

Democrats are committed to ending the "reckless and costly war of choice in Iran," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Thursday. He deferred to House Appropriations ranking member Rosa DeLauro, D-Conn., "to see what’s possible in advance of Dec. 11" in talks with the other top appropriators.

"I don’t want to get out ahead of Congresswoman DeLauro, but House Democrats have uniformly opposed providing any additional money to Donald Trump’s war machine. to Pete Hegseth’s war machine, over in the Middle East," Jeffries said.

It’s not clear how long a potential continuing resolution would last, and DeLauro said earlier this week that she wants it to be as short as possible.

The Office of Management and Budget has not yet submitted “anomalies” — changes to the current spending levels to be included in the continuing resolution — to Congress.

The administration is considering options including a stopgap bill that would run through March, sources familiar with the talks said. But no decision on the timing covered by the anomalies has been made.

Aris Folley, Jacob Fulton and Michael Macagnone contributed to this report.
